info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific

Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for

be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context: an aluminum melt made by adding AA4047 (Al-12Si) to AA6063 (Al-0.4Si-0.7Mg) was atomized into spherical powder, and we want to test how well the melt mixed by measuring Si with SEM-EDS (Thermo Fisher Apreo FE-SEM, EDAX Octane Plus silicon drift detector, 35 degree take-off angle, standards-based quantification in NIST DTSA-II against pure Al, Si and MgO standards) on powder sampled from the top, middle and bottom of the collection jar. What does it take to resolve a 1 wt% difference in Si (for example 5 versus 6 wt% Si) between two powder lots at 95% confidence?

Cover quantitatively, with citations and DOIs:
(1) Counting statistics: Ziebold's analytical-sensitivity / minimum-detectable-concentration-difference criterion (Anal. Chem. 1967) and its form in Goldstein et al. (Scanning Electron Microscopy and X-ray Microanalysis); modern SDD-EDS precision and repeatability for major and minor elements (e.g. Newbury & Ritchie); how many Si K-alpha counts per spectrum are needed, and whether counting statistics or other error sources dominate at this level.
(2) Unpolished loose spherical particles versus epoxy-mounted, polished cross-sections: magnitude of particle geometric effects (mass, absorption, fluorescence) on Si K-alpha k-ratios and concentrations, given that Si K-alpha (1.74 keV) is strongly absorbed by Al (just above the Al K edge); how much normalization to 100% or peak-to-background ratio methods (Statham; Small et al.) reduce the errors; accuracy and precision reported for particle analysis versus flat polished specimens; recommended particle size relative to the electron interaction volume at 5, 10 and 15-20 kV.
(3) Within-particle microstructural heterogeneity of rapidly solidified hypoeutectic Al-Si powder (alpha-Al cells or dendrites with eutectic Si, supersaturated solid solution) and the raster/area size or number of spots needed for a representative per-particle mean composition.
(4) Sampling statistics: how many particles per lot must be analyzed given particle-to-particle compositional variation; whether composition correlates with particle size in atomized aluminum alloy powders; segregation of powder by particle size in containers and during sampling (riffling, sample splitting), and how that could create an apparent top-versus-bottom composition difference.
(5) Published examples of EDS or electron-probe microanalysis used to assess chemical homogeneity of atomized or blended alloy powders, and how such results compared with bulk methods (ICP-OES, XRF, or X-ray diffraction lattice-parameter/phase-fraction measurements).
Note honestly where the literature is silent or values conflict.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll start by creating a comprehensive plan to address this multi-faceted question about EDS analysis of Al-Si powder.

Abstract:
Electron-excited X-ray microanalysis performed in the scanning electron microscope with energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) is a core technique for characterization of the microstructure of materials. The recent advances in EDS performance with the silicon drift detector (SDD) enable accuracy and precision equivalent to that of the high spectral resolution wavelength-dispersive spectrometer employed on the electron probe microanalyzer platform. SDD-EDS throughput, resolution, and stability provide practical operating conditions for measurement of high-count spectra that form the basis for peak fitting procedures that recover the characteristic peak intensities even for elemental combination where severe peak overlaps occur, such PbS, MoS2, BaTiO3, SrWO4, and WSi2. Accurate analyses are also demonstrated for interferences involving large concentration ratios: a major constituent on a minor constituent (Ba at 0.4299 mass fraction on Ti at 0.0180) and a major constituent on a trace constituent (Ba at 0.2194 on Ce at 0.00407; Si at 0.1145 on Ta at 0.0041). Accurate analyses of low atomic number elements, C, N, O, and F, are demonstrated. Measurement of trace constituents with limits of detection below 0.001 mass fraction (1000 ppm) is possible within a practical measurement time of 500 s.

Abstract:
As illustrated in Fig. 16.1, the physical basis of energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) with a semiconductor detector begins with photoelectric absorption of an X-ray photon in the active volume of the semiconductor (Si). The entire energy of the photon is transferred to a bound inner shell atomic electron, which is ejected with kinetic energy equal to the photon energy minus the shell ionization energy (binding energy), 1.838 keV for the Si K-shell and 0.098 keV for the Si L-shell. The ejected photoelectron undergoes inelastic scattering within the Si crystal. One of the consequences of the energy loss is the promotion of bound outer shell valence electrons to the conduction band of the semiconductor, leaving behind positively charged “holes” in the valence band. In the conduction band, the free electrons can move in response to a potential applied between the entrance surface electrode and the back surface electrode across the thickness of the Si crystal, while the positive holes in the conduction band drift in the opposite direction, resulting in the collection of electrons at the anode on the back surface of the EDS detector. This charge generation process requires approximately 3.6 eV per electron hole pair, so that the number of charge carriers is proportional to the original photon energy, Ep: 
 
$$ n={E}_p/3.6\ eV $$ 
 
For a Mn K-L3 photon with an energy of 5.895 keV, approximately 1638 electron–hole pairs are created, comprising a charge of 2.6 × 10−16 coulombs. Because the detector can respond to any photon energy from a threshold of approximately 50 eV to 30 keV or more, the process has been named “energy dispersive,” although in the spectrometry sense there is no actual dispersion such as occurs in a diffraction element spectrometer.

Abstract:
Energy dispersive X-ray microscopy (EDX) is a widely available, inexpensive method of characterizing the in-situ elemental composition of samples in Earth and life sciences. Common protocols and textbooks focussing on material sciences address EDX analysis of metallic samples that can be polished perfectly, whereas geoscientists often investigate specimens with prominent topography and composed of light, difficult to resolve elements. This is further compounded by the scarcity of literature surrounding the methodology of SEM–EDX in the field of palaeontology, leading to common misinterpretations and artefacts during data acquisition. Here, the common errors in elemental composition obtained with EDX arising from surface topography and from parameters subject to user decisions are quantified. As a model, fossil bioapatite (conodonts) and abiotic Durango apatite are used. It is shown that even microscale topography can distort measured composition by up to 34%, whereas topographic features such as tilt with respect to the electron beam lead to differences of up to 85%. Working distance was not the most important parameter affecting the results and led to differences in composition of up to 13%, whereas the choice of standard and its levelling with the sample surface led to inaccuracy reaching 33%. EDX results can be also affected by beam damage and the effects of acceleration voltage on sample acquisition and resolution are quantified. An estimate is provided of the severity of errors associated with samples which cannot satisfy preparation requirements for EDX fully, such as holotypes, and with user decisions. Using a palaeontological example, recommendations are offered for the best parameters and the relative importance of error sources are assessed.

Buckshot of a wide size, shape, and density range of mineral, glass, polymer, and metal grains, have been fired to impact perpendicularly on samples of Stardust Al 1100 foil, tightly wrapped onto aluminum alloy plate as an analogue of foil on the spacecraft collector. We have not yet been able to produce laboratory impacts by projectiles with weak and porous aggregate structure, as may occur in some cometary dust grains. In this report we present information on crater gross morphology and its dependence on particle size and density, the pre‐existing major‐ and trace‐element composition of the foil, geometrical issues for energy dispersive X‐ray analysis of the impact residues in scanning electron microscopes, and the modification of dust chemical composition during creation of impact craters as revealed by analytical transmission electron microscopy. Together, these observations help to underpin the interpretation of size, density, and composition for particles impacted on the Stardust aluminum foils.</jats:p>

Compositional characterization is essential for understanding and optimizing material performance. For powder-based materials, ubiquitous across diverse technologies, accurately resolving the composition of individual phases at high throughput remains an unsolved challenge. This bottleneck slows material research and is particularly acute for autonomous laboratories, where large numbers of samples are synthesized and AI decision-making algorithms demand low-uncertainty data. Here, we integrate measurement automation, data filtering, and unsupervised machine learning to deliver a fully automated framework for high-throughput, phase-resolved compositional analysis of as-deposited powders using scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS). Our approach, implemented in the Python-based software AutoEMXSp, overcomes geometry-induced artifacts from irregular particle morphologies and enables accurate compositional quantification using only one experimental standard per element—including light elements conventionally difficult to quantify in powders. Validated across 74 powder samples with elements spanning nitrogen to bismuth, AutoEMXSp consistently estimates compositions within 5–10% of their expected values and resolves minor or intermixed phases with high confidence. By delivering a robust, operator-free, high-throughput framework, this work paves the way for integration of powder compositional characterization into autonomous laboratory platforms, accelerating the pace of materials discovery and development.

electron-excited X-ray microanalysis. Initially useful for qualitative analysis, EDS has developed into a fully quantitative analytical tool that can match wavelength dispersive spectrometry for accuracy in the determination of major (mass concentration C > 0.1) and minor (0.01 ≤ C ≤ 0.1) constituents, and useful accuracy can extend well into the trace (0.001 < C < 0.01) constituent range even when severe peak interference occurs. Accurate analysis is possible for low atomic number elements (B, C, N, O, and F), and at low beam energy, which can optimize lateral and depth spatial resolution. By recording a full EDS spectrum at each picture element of a scan, comprehensive quantitative compositional mapping can also be performed. Abstract:
Better quality control for alloy manufacturing and sorting of post-consumer scraps relies heavily on the accurate determination of their chemical composition. In recent decades, analytical techniques, such as X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (XRF), laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), and spark optical emission spectroscopy (spark-OES), found widespread use in the metal industry, though only a few studies were published about the comparison of these techniques for commercially available alloys. Hence, we conducted a study on the evaluation of four analytical techniques (energy-dispersive XRF, wavelength-dispersive XRF, LIBS, and spark-OES) for the determination of metal sample composition. It focuses on the quantitative analysis of nine commercial alloys, representing the three most important alloy classes: copper, aluminum, and steel. First, spark-OES is proven to serve as a validation technique in the use of certified alloy reference samples. Following an examination of the lateral homogeneity by XRF, the results of the techniques are compared, and reasons for deviations are discussed. Finally, a more general evaluation of each technique with its capabilities and limitations is given, taking operation-relevant parameters, such as measurement speed and calibration effort, into account. This study shall serve as a guide for the routine use of these methods in metal producing and recycling industries.

Abstract:
The use of analytical techniques is important and critical in all areas related to REE, such as basic fundamental research, exploration, mining, extraction, and metallurgical activities at different stages by different industries. At every stage of these activities, rock, ore, minerals, and other related materials have to be analyzed for their REE contents in terms of elemental, isotopic, and mineralogical concentrations using different analytical techniques. Spectacular developments have taken place in the area of analytical instrumentation during the last four decades, with some of them having shrunk in size and become handheld. Among laboratory-based techniques, F-AAS, GF-AAS, ICP-OES, and MP-AES have become very popular. Because of high sensitivity, fewer interference effects, and ease of use, ICP-MS techniques, such as quadrupole ICP-MS, ICP-MS/MS, ICP-TOF-MS, MH-ICP-MS, HR-ICP-MS, and MC-ICP-MS, with both solution nebulization as well as direct solid analysis using laser ablation sample introduction methods, have become more popular for REE analysis. For direct analysis of solids, INAA, XRF, and LIBS techniques, as well as LA-based ICP-MS techniques, are being extensively utilized. The LIBS technique in particular requires little to no sample preparation. TIMS, SIMS, and SHRIMP techniques are being used for isotopic as well as dating REE depots. Portable analytical techniques, such as pXRF, pLIBS, and Raman spectrometers are able to perform in situ analysis even in the field, helping to make fast decisions during exploration studies. At present, hyperspectral remote sensing techniques including handheld, drone, and satellite-based techniques have become very popular in REE exploration studies because of their ability to cover larger areas in a limited time and, thus, became very cost-effective. Deployment of microanalytical devices/sensors mounted in remotely operated vehicles (ROV) is being successfully utilized in detecting REE-rich deposits in the deep oceans. Providing updated in-depth information on all these important aspects with suitable examples, especially from the point of view of REE research studies is the focal point of this review article.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Fundamental research, exploration, extraction, and metallurgical studies of rare earth elements (REEs) require the use of analytical techniques. Recently, emerging developments of analytical instrumentation for REEs have taken place, with some of them having shrunk in size, becoming handheld devices. The Flame and Graphite Furnace AAS, ICP-OES, and MP-AES are standard laboratory techniques used for the analysis of REEs. ICP-MS, ICP-MS/MS, ICP-TOF-MS, HR-ICP-MS, MH-ICP-MS, and MC-ICP-MS are popular techniques for REE analysis thanks to their ultrahigh sensitivity, minimal interference effects, and broad applicability. The INAA, XRF, LIBS, and LA-based ICP-MS techniques are widely employed for the direct analysis of solid samples. The TIMS, SIMS, and SHRIMP are common techniques used for dating isotopic REE deposits. The portable XRF, LIBS, and Raman spectrometer devices can perform on-the-spot in situ analysis, which may help make speedy decisions in the exploration study of REEs. Currently, hyperspectral remote sensing platforms, such as handheld, drone, and satellite-based devices, are preferred for the exploration of REEs due to their cost-effectiveness, which enables the coverage of large areas in a limited amount of time. The use of microanalytical sensors installed on remotely operated vehicles has been successfully applied in analyzing rich REE-bearing deposits in the deep sea. In general, this review provides in-depth information on all essential aspects, from analytical instruments to cutting-edge developments in the analysis of REE-bearing resources.</jats:p>

NL Andersen and H Winslow. A scanning electron microscope-energy dispersive spectrometry (sem-eds) method for the quantitative analysis of common volcanic phases. Unknown journal, Unknown year.

The excerpt provides empirical counting-statistics information for SEM-EDS but does not mention Ziebold’s analytical-sensitivity formulation or state an explicit number of counts required to achieve 1 wt% precision. Under the reported standard conditions (15 kV, approximately 3 nA, 16 µs process time), spectra containing about 1.5 × 10^6 counts gave reproducible glass-standard results: oxides above 10 wt% generally had relative standard deviations (RSDs) below 1–2%, while most components between 1 and 10 wt% had RSDs below 2%. The authors emphasize that detection limits depend strongly on total spectrum counts, element, and matrix. Their estimated detection limits at 1.5 × 10^6 counts were 0.04–0.08 wt% for Ca and lower-energy peaks and 0.09–0.19 wt% for higher-energy peaks. Reducing acquisitions to approximately 0.25 × 10^6 counts improved resistance to beam damage but degraded precision, especially for minor elements. Thus, the passage supports approximately 1.5 million counts as an experimental condition yielding roughly percent-level precision for many major and intermediate-concentration oxides, but it cannot establish a universal count requirement for 1 wt% precision.

The excerpt discusses EDS analytical sensitivity and detection limits using counting statistics, but it does not state a specific number of counts required to achieve 1 wt% precision. It defines trace elements as constituents below a mass concentration of 0.01 and notes that, when peak overlap is insignificant, limits of detection of approximately 0.0002–0.0005 mass concentration (200–500 ppm) can be obtained, depending on the element and matrix, with counting times under 500 seconds. The cited detection-limit expression is CDL = [3NB^1/2/(NS − NB)]CS, where NB is the background count beneath the peak, NS is the integrated peak count, and CS is the known or measured trace concentration. Thus, the relevant counting requirement depends not only on total counts but also on background, net peak intensity, matrix composition, and spectral interference. The excerpt also describes an extreme trace-analysis example with a spectrum integral of 1.7 billion counts, involving constituents near 500 ppm, but this is an example of high-sensitivity measurement rather than a general precision rule. No direct Ziebold relationship or explicit 1 wt% precision count requirement appears in these pages.

The excerpt discusses EDS counting statistics, sensitivity, and detection limits, but it does not specifically cite Ziebold or state the number of counts required for 1 wt% precision. It recommends collecting spectra with approximately 10^7 integrated counts for accurate low-level quantification, while noting that SDD-EDS can produce spectra exceeding 50 million counts in practical counting times. Such high counts lower the minimum detectable concentration to substantially below 0.001 mass fraction (1000 ppm). The excerpt also gives a concentration-limit-of-detection relationship involving the background counts (NB), the measured peak intensity (NS), and the known concentration of a standard (CS): CDL = 3 sqrt(NB)/(NS − NB) × CS. For ideal Poisson counting of a net peak, relative statistical uncertainty scales approximately as 1/sqrt(N), so a 1% counting-statistical precision would conventionally correspond to roughly 10,000 net counts; however, that numerical inference is not explicitly stated in this excerpt and practical EDS precision also depends on background, overlaps, deadtime, matrix corrections, and calibration.

The excerpt documents high-precision, standards-based quantitative SDD-EDS analysis using NIST DTSA-II. Measurements were acquired at 20 keV for 50 seconds, yielding approximately 5 million counts, and processed with multiple linear least-squares peak fitting. Pure Mg, Si, and Fe standards and NIST SRM 470 glass as the Ca standard were used to measure intensities and form k-values; concentrations were then calculated using the XPP matrix-correction procedure in DTSA-II. For 20 randomly selected locations on polished NIST SRM 470 (K411 glass), measured averages agreed with certified SRM values within 1.7% relative. The reported single-measurement relative standard deviations were approximately 0.11% for Mg, 0.079% for Si, 0.089% for Ca, and 0.26% for Fe, while 20-location relative standard deviations were 0.5%, 0.21%, 0.23%, and 0.275%, respectively. The paper defines major constituents as above 10 weight percent and minor constituents as between 1 and 10 weight percent. It emphasizes that this accuracy and repeatability apply to the ideal polished bulk geometry; rough, irregular, or particle specimens can compromise standards-based k-ratio quantification.

Detection limits can reach approximately 0.0005 mass fraction for many elements. Tables 13–16 demonstrate repeatability and agreement with ideal stoichiometry for carbides, nitrides, oxides, and fluorides; replicate scatter values (r) are generally small, supporting high precision under controlled conditions. Table 17 reports NIST K497 glass detection limits from 41–329 ppm for selected elements under a 500-second acquisition, with uncertainties listed for each CDL. Achieving EPMA/WDS-level results requires careful measurement science, including polished unknowns and standards with surface relief below 50 nm rms. The excerpt emphasizes that specimen topography, local inclination, and thickness can cause severe quantitative errors. In the pyrite example analyzed with DTSA-II, k-ratio and matrix-correction results provide a warning through the raw analytical total, whereas standardless analysis can conceal topographic problems. The excerpt directly describes the peak-to-background (P/B) ratio method for quantitative EDS analysis of particles and rough, non-bulk geometries. Conventional EDS assumes a flat bulk sample that fully contains the X-ray generation volume, whereas loose particles introduce geometry-dependent effects. The P/B approach compensates for these effects by exploiting the approximate invariance of the peak-to-background ratio between particle and bulk samples of identical composition. Particle peak and background intensities are measured, and the particle peak intensity is transformed into a geometry-corrected, bulk-equivalent intensity suitable for conventional quantification models. The method therefore addresses geometry artifacts arising from particle shape, finite size, absorption, and substrate-related effects. The implementation described here improves background modeling by accounting for continuum generation, absorption, backscattering, detector response, and geometry-dependent X-ray path lengths. It also incorporates electron stopping-power effects when estimating the bulk reference background, reducing errors when the standard and unknown sample have substantially different average atomic numbers. These corrections allow a single experimental standard per element to be used across samples with widely varying compositions. The excerpt does not explicitly identify Statham and Small by name, but it presents the relevant conceptual basis and refinements of the P/B method for particle-level quantitative EDS.

Elemental mass fractions are calculated by comparing the characteristic peak-to-background ratio from a particle with that from an experimental standard, with corrections for backscattering (Rc), absorption (Ac), secondary fluorescence (Fc), and continuum-generation differences (Zc). The Zc term is particularly important because the generated continuum intensity can differ substantially between a particle and its standard as a function of average atomic number, potentially varying by 20–500%. The excerpt emphasizes that the true matrix-free continuum-generation term is not simply the empirical background function fB; instead, it is calculated as Bgen = fB · S, including a stopping-power correction. For compounds, the average atomic number is computed using the Statham formulation, which outperforms simple mass-weighted alternatives and supports use of one standard per element. To address geometry artifacts in irregular particles, the conventional flat-surface X-ray path is modified with fitted geometric parameters z0 and m: ℓ(z) = (z + z·m + z0)csc Ψ. Positive parameter values represent increased absorption and negative values reduced absorption relative to a flat sample. This provides an approximate correction for surface tilt and positional offset along the detector path.

Amber Lynn Genau. Microstructural development in al-si powder during rapid solidification. ArXiv, Dec 2004. URL: https://doi.org/10.2172/835374, doi:10.2172/835374. This article has 7 citations.

The excerpt describes microstructural heterogeneity in rapidly solidified hypoeutectic Al–Si particles, specifically Al–3 wt% Si and Al–6 wt% Si. Particles in the 0.1–1.0 μm range commonly exhibited three successive microstructural regions. Initially, rapid growth produced a supersaturated α-Al solid solution with a planar interface, followed by precipitation of very fine Si clusters. During recalescence, reduced solute-trapping capability created a segregate-free zone and increased Si supersaturation ahead of the interface. As solidification progressed, the planar interface became unstable and transformed into a cellular structure, providing qualitative evidence for cell formation and microstructural heterogeneity. Smaller particles were more likely to remain segregation-free because they experienced greater undercooling and higher solid/liquid interface velocities; conversely, large faceted Si crystals were more frequently observed in larger, higher-Si particles. The excerpt does not provide a direct quantitative cell-size-versus-particle-size relationship or explicit cooling-rate data for these powders. It does state that eutectic, microcellular, and dendrite-arm spacings can be used as indirect measures of interface temperature and velocity. Jackson–Hunt and TMK models relate eutectic spacing to growth velocity and undercooling, with the TMK extension being more appropriate when rapid solidification raises the Peclet number above unity.

The excerpt provides a framework for interpreting microstructural heterogeneity in rapidly solidified Al-Si powder. Particle size strongly affects cooling: smaller particles have a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio, cool more rapidly, and generally reach greater undercooling. Greater undercooling increases the solidification driving force and interface velocity, so particle size can influence dendrite or cellular scale and the development of eutectic segregation. Atomization gas is also important; helium promotes faster cooling than nitrogen because of its greater heat capacity, thermal conductivity, and heat-transfer coefficient. The thermal history of an atomized droplet commonly includes an initial adiabatic stage, during which recalescence reheats the particle and the interface velocity decreases, followed by slower, approximately isothermal growth controlled by external heat loss. This change in growth conditions can produce different morphologies or segregation spacings at different positions within one particle, contributing to microstructural heterogeneity. Under sufficiently extreme undercooling, a particle can enter the hypercooled regime, where recalescence does not restore the temperature to the melting point and segregation may be absent. The excerpt does not give specific quantitative relationships for alpha-Al dendrite fraction, eutectic Si spacing, supersaturated solid solution, or cell size versus particle size, but it establishes cooling rate, undercooling, gas choice, and changing interface velocity as the controlling factors.

Abstract:
Metallic powders are widely utilized as feedstock materials in metal additive manufacturing (MAM). However, only a limited number of alloys can currently be processed using these technologies, with most of them being casting alloys. The objective of this study is to investigate novel aluminum alloys produced via a close-coupled gas atomizer (CCGA) by adding an increasing amount of copper (4, 8, and 20 wt%) to an AlSi10Mg alloy. The obtained powders were fully characterized to evaluate the effect of copper, a well-established strengthener for aluminum alloys, in order to correlate the obtained hardness to the powder phase composition and microstructure. In particular, a dendritic microstructure was observed in all alloys, and, as the copper content was increased, the size of the secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) decreased progressively. Consequently, the hardness measured on the powder cross-section linearly increased with the copper content, and the hardness value of 185 ± 13 HV of the AlCu20Si10Mg composition was found to be twice that of the AlSi10Mg alloy (88 ± 5 HV).

Abstract:
In this study, the comparison of properties between fresh (virgin) and used (recycled) 316L stainless steel (316L SS) and AlSi10Mg powders for the laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing (L-PBF AM) process has been investigated in detail. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) techniques are used to determine and evaluate the evolution of morphology, particle size distribution (PSD), circularity, chemical composition, and phase (crystal structure) in the virgin and recycled powders of both materials. The results indicate that both recycled powders increase the average particle sizes and shift the PSD to higher values, compared with their virgin powders. The recycled 316L SS powder particles largely retain their spherical and near-spherical morphologies, whereas more irregularly shaped morphologies are observed for the recycled AlSi10Mg counterpart. The average circularity of recycled 316L SS powder only reduces by ~2%, but decreases ~17% for the recycled AlSi10Mg powder. EDX analysis confirms that both recycled powders retain their alloy-specific chemical compositions, but with increased oxygen content. XRD spectra peak analysis suggests that there are no phase change and no presence of any undesired precipitates in both recycled powders. Based on qualitative comparative analysis between the current results and from various available literature, the reuse of both recycled powders is acceptable up to 30 times, but re-evaluation through physical and chemical characterizations of the powders is advised, if they are to be subjected for further reuse.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing opens new possibilities for designing light-weight structures using aluminium alloys. The microstructure of two Al alloys and their corrosion resistance in NaCl and natural seawater environments were investigated. The newly designed Al-Mn-Cr-Zr based alloy showed a higher corrosion resistance than reference AlSi10Mg alloy in both environments in as printed and heat-treated conditions. The corrosion initiated in the Al matrix along the precipitates in the alloys where the Volta potential difference was found the highest. The coarser microstructure and precipitate composition of the new Al-alloy led to the formation of a resistant passive film which extended the passivity region of the Al-Mn-Cr-Zr alloy compared to the AlSi10Mg alloy. The effect of heat treatment could be seen in the microstructure as more precipitates were found in between the melt pool boundaries, which affected the corrosion initiation and slightly the pitting resistance. Overall, this study shows that a newly designed Al-alloy for additive manufacturing has a suitable corrosion resistance for applications in marine environments.

Amber Lynn Genau. Microstructural development in al-si powder during rapid solidification. ArXiv, Dec 2004. URL: https://doi.org/10.2172/835374, doi:10.2172/835374. This article has 7 citations.

The excerpt links particle size to cooling rate and the resulting solidification behavior in gas-atomized aluminum-silicon powders. As particle diameter decreases, the surface-area-to-volume ratio increases, causing a higher convective cooling rate. Fine particles therefore experience greater undercooling, which increases the driving force for solidification and produces a faster solid-liquid interface velocity. Gas choice also affects this relationship: helium, owing to its higher heat capacity, thermal conductivity, and heat-transfer coefficient, produces faster particle cooling than heavier gases. The excerpt describes two thermal regimes in typical atomized droplets. Initially, particles may solidify adiabatically, with recalescence reheating the droplet; as the interface slows, segregation spacing changes across the particle diameter. Later growth becomes slower and approximately isothermal as external heat loss controls solidification. Thus, coarse and fine particles can develop different microstructural and segregation characteristics, while a single particle may show changing segregation spacing from its nucleation region outward. At extremely high undercooling, fine droplets may enter the hypercooled regime, where recalescence cannot restore the particle to the melting temperature and segregation is absent. The passage does not provide direct measured solute-composition differences between fine and coarse powder fractions, but it establishes the cooling-rate and particle-size mechanisms expected to control segregation.

The excerpt indicates a clear particle-size effect on composition and solute segregation during rapid solidification of aluminum–silicon droplets. Smaller particles are more likely to solidify with little or no segregation because their greater cooling rate promotes larger undercooling and faster solid/liquid interface velocity. These conditions enhance solute trapping and can suppress the development of compositional differences during solidification. The excerpt also describes a sequence in which an initially supersaturated solid solution forms under planar growth; as recalescence occurs, the driving force for solute trapping decreases, producing a segregate-free zone and increasing silicon supersaturation ahead of the interface, followed by cellular breakdown. At sufficiently high undercooling, droplets can enter the hypercooled regime, where recalescence is insufficient to bring the temperature to the liquidus and no segregation is expected. Conversely, larger particles cool more slowly and are more likely to develop segregated or heterogeneous structures. Large faceted silicon crystals were observed more frequently in larger particles, particularly at higher silicon contents. Thus, the source supports an inverse relationship between particle size and cooling rate, with fine particles experiencing faster cooling, greater undercooling, and reduced solute segregation, while coarse particles experience slower cooling and greater opportunity for segregation or silicon-rich phase formation.

Although low liquid fractions, small grain size, and high cooling rates are generally expected to suppress segregation, significant macro-segregation can still occur. The proposed mechanism is inverse segregation: during solidification, solute-rich residual liquid is drawn through the solid network by solidification shrinkage and, in rotating sprayforming, is driven outward by centrifugal force. For solutes with partition coefficients below one, this produces depletion near the billet center and enrichment near the surface. The excerpt reports that liquid fraction can range from nearly zero to above 60%, with approximately 10–30% typically needed for acceptable metallurgical quality. It also distinguishes elements forming dispersoid particles: these do not segregate because they become locked into the solid network. Thus, the passage supports a qualitative correlation between cooling/solidification conditions and segregation, but not a quantitative relationship between gas-atomized particle size and solute concentration in fine and coarse particles.

The excerpt explains that lowering accelerating voltage reduces the electron interaction and x-ray generation volumes inside particles. At 20 kV, electrons interact through much of a 2–3 µm glass microsphere, with substantial scattering from the sides and bottom and x-ray generation near the particle edges. Consequently, measured intensities depend on particle size and shape and require corrections for particle mass and absorption. At 5 kV, the interaction and x-ray generation volumes are much smaller; for the illustrated microspheres, the effects of particle geometry become minimal and the particle behaves more like a bulk material. The study experimentally examined bulk glass, microspheres, and irregular shards using several accelerating voltages. Microspheres were measured at 5 kV and 10 kV for 500 seconds, and at 15 kV and 25 kV for 300 seconds. Irregular K-411 shards were also analyzed at 10, 17, 20, 22, and 25 kV. Thus, the excerpt directly supports the relationship between particle size and interaction volume and identifies 5 kV as the condition producing the smallest interaction volume and least geometric influence. It reports measurements at 10, 15, and 25 kV, but does not by itself establish a universal recommendation among all requested energies.

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a summary table of the key error sources and their approximate magnitudes when measuring Si by SEM-EDS in atomized Al-Si powder for a 1 wt% concentration difference at 95% confidence. Include the following rows: (1) Counting statistics (Poisson) - requirement and typical performance, (2) Matrix correction / standards-based accuracy on flat polished specimens, (3) Particle geometry effects (mass, absorption) at 10 kV, 15 kV, 20 kV, (4) P/B correction performance on loose powder, (5) Within-particle microstructural heterogeneity (SDAS ~2 \u00b5m), (6) Particle-to-particle compositional scatter, (7) Sampling/size segregation in containers. For each row, show the error source, typical magnitude of the error contribution (as absolute wt% or relative %), whether it is random or systematic, and whether it is the dominant barrier to resolving 1 wt% Si. Draw from the evidence collected from Newbury & Ritchie 2015/2019, Small 2002, Giunto et al. 2026, Trivedi 2003, Genau 2004, Vanzetti 2023, Neikov 2019, etc."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Error source / condition | Approximate magnitude relevant to 5–6 wt% Si | Error character | Dominant barrier to resolving 1 wt% Si? |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Counting statistics (Poisson; two independent spectra) | For a 1 wt% difference at 95% confidence, the counting-only requirement is about **426 net Si Kα counts per spectrum** if background is negligible: \(1.96\sqrt{5^2/N+6^2/N}\le1\). A conservative target of **≥1,000 net counts** gives an approximate 95% uncertainty of **±0.32–0.37 wt% per spectrum** at 5–6 wt% Si; **10,000 counts** gives about **±0.10–0.12 wt%**. Background subtraction increases the requirement. Modern high-count SDD spectra readily exceed this level (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004) | Random; reducible by counts and replicates | **No**, once ≥1,000–10,000 net Si counts are collected; geometry, microstructure, and particle sampling then dominate |
| Standards-based k-ratio/matrix correction on a flat, polished specimen | Si repeatability of **0.079% relative** for single measurements on K411 glass; approximately **0.21% relative** across 20 locations. Fe–3Si gave **0.24% relative** replicate precision. Across 50 major/minor determinations, **84% were within ±2% relative** of reference values—about **±0.10–0.12 wt% at 5–6 wt% Si**—although routine accuracy guidance is broader (about ±10% relative for minor constituents) (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) | Small random repeatability plus systematic standards/matrix-model uncertainty | **Usually no** for a controlled polished mount, but a measured 1 wt% difference should be confirmed by batch QC and preferably bulk chemistry |
| Loose-particle geometry at **10 kV** | For approximately 0.9–18 µm glass spheres, particle/bulk ratios were generally within **0.9–1.1** above about 1.4 µm; irregular-shard composition variation was about **8–12% relative**, corresponding roughly to **0.4–0.7 wt% Si** at 5–6 wt% (pqac-00000075, pqac-00000076, pqac-00000077) | Particle-position-dependent random scatter with systematic size/shape bias | **Potentially**, especially without size matching, center targeting, filtering, or particle-specific correction |
| Loose-particle geometry at **15 kV** | Mass-effect loss reached about **13%** for a 1.8 µm sphere; particle/bulk response approached unity only above roughly 3 µm. Low-energy Si Kα absorption artifacts were larger than at 10 kV, so biases of order **≥0.6 wt% at 5 wt% Si** are plausible for small particles (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000076) | Systematic with particle diameter and detector-facing geometry; additional random placement scatter | **Yes** for small or broadly sized loose particles |
| Loose-particle geometry at **20 kV** | Direct 20 kV values were not isolated in the retrieved microsphere results; behavior lies between 15 and 25 kV. At 20 kV, a 2–3 µm sphere is penetrated through much of its volume, with electron escape and edge generation; at 25 kV, 1–2 µm spheres lost **50–75%** of high-energy intensity and Si particle/bulk ratios reached about **1.4**. Thus 20 kV can readily cause **tens-of-percent relative** errors for particles only a few micrometres across (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000072) | Strong systematic size/shape/absorption bias plus position-dependent scatter | **Yes—often overwhelmingly** for loose particles comparable to the interaction volume |
| Peak-to-background (P/B) correction on loose powder | Earlier particle P/B work commonly achieved about **10–20% relative error**; a modern modified P/B workflow on 74 raw powder materials generally achieved **5–10% relative deviation**, equivalent to roughly **0.25–0.60 wt% at 5–6 wt% Si**. It reduces but does not eliminate tilt, absorption, substrate, roughness, and finite-size errors (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000044) | Residual systematic bias plus particle-to-particle scatter | **Borderline**: adequate for screening a 1 wt% shift with many accepted particles, but weaker than polished-section analysis |
| Within-particle Al–Si microstructural heterogeneity | AlSi10Mg powder had mean secondary dendrite-arm spacing **2.19 ± 0.56 µm**; Si is enriched in the interdendritic/eutectic network, while rapidly solidified α-Al can be supersaturated and contain nanoscale Si. Point analyses can therefore range from Al-rich cells to Si-rich eutectic by many wt%; spatial morphology and spacing also change within one droplet (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000065) | Real spatial heterogeneity; random only if locations are sampled without bias | **Yes** for spot analyses; largely controlled by a representative raster spanning many cells or whole cross-section |
| Particle-to-particle compositional scatter | No universal value exists for atomized Al–Si powder. Modern automated powder EDS found 48.1% of benchmark elemental distributions with SD <1 at% and 91.2% <2 at%, but these data cover diverse chemistries, not specifically Al–Si. Particle size, nucleation, solute trapping, and cooling history can create real between-particle differences (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000071) | Real random-effects variance, potentially size-dependent | **Often yes**; particle count must be selected from the observed SD, not from counting statistics alone |
| Sampling and size segregation in jars/containers | Sampling-method variability reported as **6.81% for quartering**, **5.14% for scoop sampling**, **1.01% for chute splitting**, and **0.146% for rotary division**. Vibration and flow can segregate particle sizes; fine Al–Si droplets cool faster and exhibit more solute trapping/less segregation, so a size gradient can become an apparent top–bottom chemistry gradient (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000065) | Systematic lot-location bias plus sampling variance | **Yes** unless each jar level is independently split with a rotary divider and results are stratified or matched by particle size |


*Table: Approximate error magnitudes and dominant limitations for distinguishing 5 from 6 wt% Si in atomized aluminum powder. The comparison shows that adequate Si counts are easy to obtain, while loose-particle geometry, microstructural heterogeneity, particle sampling, and size segregation usually control the result.*

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table of recommended experimental protocols for resolving a 1 wt% Si difference between two powder lots at 95% confidence. Include columns for: Protocol Element, Recommendation, Rationale/Literature Support. Rows should include: (1) Specimen preparation (polished cross-section vs loose particles), (2) Accelerating voltage choice, (3) Spectrum acquisition parameters (counts, deadtime, live time), (4) Quantification method (standards-based k-ratio with DTSA-II vs P/B), (5) Raster/area size for representative per-particle composition, (6) Number of particles per lot, (7) Powder sampling method (riffling), (8) Particle size stratification, (9) Confirmation by bulk method. Base on evidence from Newbury & Ritchie, Small, Giunto et al., Vanzetti, Neikov, Trivedi/Genau."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Protocol element | Recommendation | Rationale / literature support |
|---|---|---|
| Specimen preparation | **Primary method:** Embed each independently split subsample in low-viscosity epoxy, vacuum-impregnate, grind, and polish through particle equators to a flat finish. Carbon-coat mounts and standards similarly. Randomize fields and exclude particles intersecting mount edges or pores. Use loose particles only for screening or when polishing is impossible. | Standards-based EDS assumes flat bulk geometry. Polished standards produced approximately 0.08–0.26% relative single-measurement precision and about 0.2% spatial RSD for Si, whereas scratches, shards, and particles generated broad errors approaching an order of magnitude. Normalization to 100% can hide these errors (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000017). |
| Accelerating voltage | For polished Al–Si sections, begin at **10 kV** and verify the result at **15 kV** on a subset. Use 15–20 kV only when particles are comfortably larger than the interaction volume and additional count rate is needed. For loose particles, prefer **10 kV** and particles larger than approximately 3–5 µm; 5 kV may reduce geometry effects further but is more sensitive to contamination and low overvoltage. | At 10 kV, approximately 0.9–18 µm glass spheres generally gave particle-to-bulk ratios within 0.9–1.1 above about 1.4 µm. At 15 kV, a 1.8 µm sphere lost about 13% intensity; at 25 kV, 1–2 µm spheres lost 50–75%, and Si Kα particle-to-bulk ratios reached about 1.4. Ten kilovolts gave the lowest variation for irregular shards; 5 kV suffered contamination-related bias (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000072, pqac-00000075, pqac-00000077). |
| Spectrum acquisition | Acquire **at least 10,000 background-corrected Si Kα counts per accepted particle mean**; 20,000–50,000 is preferable when time permits. Keep detector dead time near **10% and below 15%**, monitor beam current with a Faraday cup or reference standard, bracket each session with a homogeneous Al–Si control, and use identical conditions for standards and unknowns. Determine live time empirically from the Si count rate. | Ten thousand net counts limit ideal Poisson relative uncertainty to about 1%, or approximately 0.05–0.06 wt% at 5–6 wt% Si. High-count SDD spectra readily achieve sub-percent repeatability, so geometry, microstructure, and sampling—not counting statistics—should dominate. Excess dead time increases coincidence artifacts; stable beam dose is required for rigorous k-ratios (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000057). |
| Quantification | Use the existing **standards-based k-ratio/DTSA-II** procedure with pure Al and Si standards and matched beam conditions; retain both normalized composition and the **raw analytical total**. If available, analyze an Al–Si reference alloy near 5–6 wt% Si as independent QC. For loose particles, use a validated **peak-to-local-background method** with particle filtering rather than ordinary bulk ZAF alone. | DTSA-II standards-based analysis placed 84% of 50 major/minor determinations within ±2% relative of reference values. Raw totals near 98–102% are a useful geometry diagnostic; normalization alone can conceal anomalous absorption. Modified P/B methods reduce finite-size and topographic effects but generally retain about 5–10% relative error on raw particles, versus roughly 2–5% for well-prepared standards or polished specimens (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000044). |
| Per-particle raster or area | On polished sections, raster nearly the **entire exposed particle cross-section**, remaining at least one interaction radius from epoxy and neighboring particles. If whole-section rastering is impractical, combine systematically distributed fields whose total span covers at least **5–10 dendrite or cell spacings**—approximately **10–20 µm** for an AlSi10Mg-like spacing of 2.19 µm—and include the particle center and rim. Do not use one arbitrary point as the particle mean. | Rapidly solidified Al–Si particles contain α-Al cells or dendrites, Si-rich interdendritic eutectic, supersaturated Al, and nanoscale Si. Morphology and spacing can change across one droplet. Reported AlSi10Mg secondary dendrite-arm spacing was 2.19 ± 0.56 µm, while Si was concentrated in interdendritic networks (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000065). |
| Number of particles per lot | Analyze an initial **30 randomly selected particles per lot**, then estimate between-particle SD, `s_p`, from per-particle means. For two equal-sized independent lots, use at minimum `n ≥ 2(1.96s_p/1.0)²` particles per lot for a 95% CI on a 1 wt% difference; for 80% power use `n ≥ 2(1.96 + 0.84)²s_p²`. The confidence criterion gives approximately **8, 18, and 31 particles per lot** for `s_p = 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 wt%`, respectively. In practice, use **at least 30 and preferably 50–100 particles per lot**. Treat particles—not spectra or spots—as independent replicates. | Published powder studies support averaging many spectra but do not provide a universal particle count for atomized Al–Si. Automated powder EDS showed that cluster averaging improved agreement with expected composition, while real particle-to-particle variance depends on particle size, nucleation, and solute trapping. Sample size must therefore be calculated from observed particle variance rather than X-ray counts (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000071). |
| Powder sampling and splitting | Treat top, middle, and bottom as three separately collected strata. Take several increments across each stratum, combine them, gently homogenize without grinding, and reduce each composite with a **rotary sample divider** or validated multi-chute riffle splitter. Prepare at least **two independent splits and mounts per stratum**; do not scoop the analytical portion directly from the jar. | Reported subdivision variability was about 0.146% for rotary division and 1.01% for chute splitting, compared with 5.14% for scoop sampling and 6.81% for quartering. Vibration, funnel flow, and sifting can produce vertical size segregation in stored powder (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040). |
| Particle-size stratification | Measure every analyzed particle’s equivalent diameter and assign predefined size bins. Compare lots both **within common size bins** and after reweighting to a common particle-size distribution. Also sieve representative bulk splits and analyze at least fine, middle, and coarse fractions independently. Include size and a lot-by-size interaction in the statistical model. | Fine droplets cool faster, undercool more, and exhibit greater solute trapping and less segregation; coarse droplets more readily form segregated structures. Published fine and coarse AlSi10Mg powders differed nominally in Si—8.56 versus 9.76 wt%—although this alone does not prove atomization segregation. Jar size segregation can therefore mimic a top-to-bottom Si gradient (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000068, pqac-00000069). |
| Statistical comparison | Fit a hierarchical model or mixed-effects ANOVA with **jar stratum or lot as the fixed effect**, size bin as a covariate, and split, mount, and particle as nested random effects. Report the top-minus-bottom estimate with its 95% CI, variance components, rejected-spectrum fraction, and sensitivity analysis with and without size adjustment. Claim resolution only when the 95% CI excludes zero and is sufficiently narrow to distinguish the specified 1 wt% contrast. | Repeated spectra on one particle improve counting precision but do not increase the number of independently sampled particles.
