# Resolving a 1 wt% Si Difference in Atomized Al–Si Powder by SEM-EDS: A Quantitative Assessment

## Overview

Distinguishing 5 from 6 wt% Si between two lots of gas-atomized hypoeutectic Al–Si powder at 95% confidence requires controlling five largely independent sources of uncertainty: (1) X-ray counting statistics, (2) particle geometry effects versus flat-specimen assumptions, (3) within-particle microstructural heterogeneity, (4) particle-to-particle compositional scatter, and (5) physical sampling of the powder jar. The following analysis draws on published literature to quantify each contribution and identify the dominant barriers.

The table below summarizes the approximate magnitudes of these error sources and whether each is likely to be the dominant barrier to resolving a 1 wt% Si difference.

| Error source / condition | Approximate magnitude relevant to 5–6 wt% Si | Error character | Dominant barrier to resolving 1 wt% Si? |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Counting statistics (Poisson; two independent spectra) | For a 1 wt% difference at 95% confidence, the counting-only requirement is about **426 net Si Kα counts per spectrum** if background is negligible: \(1.96\sqrt{5^2/N+6^2/N}\le1\). A conservative target of **≥1,000 net counts** gives an approximate 95% uncertainty of **±0.32–0.37 wt% per spectrum** at 5–6 wt% Si; **10,000 counts** gives about **±0.10–0.12 wt%**. Background subtraction increases the requirement. Modern high-count SDD spectra readily exceed this level (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004) | Random; reducible by counts and replicates | **No**, once ≥1,000–10,000 net Si counts are collected; geometry, microstructure, and particle sampling then dominate |
| Standards-based k-ratio/matrix correction on a flat, polished specimen | Si repeatability of **0.079% relative** for single measurements on K411 glass; approximately **0.21% relative** across 20 locations. Fe–3Si gave **0.24% relative** replicate precision. Across 50 major/minor determinations, **84% were within ±2% relative** of reference values—about **±0.10–0.12 wt% at 5–6 wt% Si**—although routine accuracy guidance is broader (about ±10% relative for minor constituents) (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) | Small random repeatability plus systematic standards/matrix-model uncertainty | **Usually no** for a controlled polished mount, but a measured 1 wt% difference should be confirmed by batch QC and preferably bulk chemistry |
| Loose-particle geometry at **10 kV** | For approximately 0.9–18 µm glass spheres, particle/bulk ratios were generally within **0.9–1.1** above about 1.4 µm; irregular-shard composition variation was about **8–12% relative**, corresponding roughly to **0.4–0.7 wt% Si** at 5–6 wt% (pqac-00000075, pqac-00000076, pqac-00000077) | Particle-position-dependent random scatter with systematic size/shape bias | **Potentially**, especially without size matching, center targeting, filtering, or particle-specific correction |
| Loose-particle geometry at **15 kV** | Mass-effect loss reached about **13%** for a 1.8 µm sphere; particle/bulk response approached unity only above roughly 3 µm. Low-energy Si Kα absorption artifacts were larger than at 10 kV, so biases of order **≥0.6 wt% at 5 wt% Si** are plausible for small particles (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000076) | Systematic with particle diameter and detector-facing geometry; additional random placement scatter | **Yes** for small or broadly sized loose particles |
| Loose-particle geometry at **20 kV** | Direct 20 kV values were not isolated in the retrieved microsphere results; behavior lies between 15 and 25 kV. At 20 kV, a 2–3 µm sphere is penetrated through much of its volume, with electron escape and edge generation; at 25 kV, 1–2 µm spheres lost **50–75%** of high-energy intensity and Si particle/bulk ratios reached about **1.4**. Thus 20 kV can readily cause **tens-of-percent relative** errors for particles only a few micrometres across (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000072) | Strong systematic size/shape/absorption bias plus position-dependent scatter | **Yes—often overwhelmingly** for loose particles comparable to the interaction volume |
| Peak-to-background (P/B) correction on loose powder | Earlier particle P/B work commonly achieved about **10–20% relative error**; a modern modified P/B workflow on 74 raw powder materials generally achieved **5–10% relative deviation**, equivalent to roughly **0.25–0.60 wt% at 5–6 wt% Si**. It reduces but does not eliminate tilt, absorption, substrate, roughness, and finite-size errors (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000044) | Residual systematic bias plus particle-to-particle scatter | **Borderline**: adequate for screening a 1 wt% shift with many accepted particles, but weaker than polished-section analysis |
| Within-particle Al–Si microstructural heterogeneity | AlSi10Mg powder had mean secondary dendrite-arm spacing **2.19 ± 0.56 µm**; Si is enriched in the interdendritic/eutectic network, while rapidly solidified α-Al can be supersaturated and contain nanoscale Si. Point analyses can therefore range from Al-rich cells to Si-rich eutectic by many wt%; spatial morphology and spacing also change within one droplet (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000065) | Real spatial heterogeneity; random only if locations are sampled without bias | **Yes** for spot analyses; largely controlled by a representative raster spanning many cells or whole cross-section |
| Particle-to-particle compositional scatter | No universal value exists for atomized Al–Si powder. Modern automated powder EDS found 48.1% of benchmark elemental distributions with SD <1 at% and 91.2% <2 at%, but these data cover diverse chemistries, not specifically Al–Si. Particle size, nucleation, solute trapping, and cooling history can create real between-particle differences (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000071) | Real random-effects variance, potentially size-dependent | **Often yes**; particle count must be selected from the observed SD, not from counting statistics alone |
| Sampling and size segregation in jars/containers | Sampling-method variability reported as **6.81% for quartering**, **5.14% for scoop sampling**, **1.01% for chute splitting**, and **0.146% for rotary division**. Vibration and flow can segregate particle sizes; fine Al–Si droplets cool faster and exhibit more solute trapping/less segregation, so a size gradient can become an apparent top–bottom chemistry gradient (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000065) | Systematic lot-location bias plus sampling variance | **Yes** unless each jar level is independently split with a rotary divider and results are stratified or matched by particle size |


*Table: Approximate error magnitudes and dominant limitations for distinguishing 5 from 6 wt% Si in atomized aluminum powder. The comparison shows that adequate Si counts are easy to obtain, while loose-particle geometry, microstructural heterogeneity, particle sampling, and size segregation usually control the result.*

---

## (1) Counting Statistics: Ziebold's Criterion and Modern SDD-EDS Performance

### Ziebold's Analytical Sensitivity

Ziebold (Anal. Chem. 39, 858–861, 1967; DOI: 10.1021/ac60252a028) defined the analytical sensitivity ΔC as the minimum concentration difference resolvable at a given confidence level, governed by Poisson counting statistics. For two measurements of a constituent at concentration C, the minimum resolvable difference at 95% confidence is approximately ΔC ≈ 2 × 1.96 × σ_C, where σ_C depends on the net peak counts N, the peak-to-background ratio, and the concentration itself. In the formulation retained by Goldstein et al. (Scanning Electron Microscopy and X-ray Microanalysis, Springer, 2018; DOI: 10.1007/978-1-4939-6676-9), the concentration detection limit is expressed as C_DL = (3√N_B / (N_S − N_B)) × C_S, where N_B is the background count beneath the peak, N_S is the total integrated count in the peak channel window, and C_S is the known standard concentration (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002).

### Counts Needed for Si Kα

For a constituent near 5–6 wt%, the relative statistical precision on a single measurement scales as approximately 1/√N, where N is the net characteristic peak count. To achieve a 1% relative counting precision (approximately ±0.05–0.06 wt% at 5–6 wt% Si), one needs roughly 10,000 net Si Kα counts per spectrum. For a cruder 5% relative precision (about ±0.25–0.30 wt%), approximately 400 net counts suffice. A two-sample test comparing 5 versus 6 wt% Si at 95% confidence purely from counting statistics requires modestly more than this, but the requirement is easily met: modern SDD-EDS systems routinely accumulate total spectrum integrals of 10⁶–10⁷ counts in 30–60 seconds of live time, yielding well over 10,000 Si Kα counts in an Al–5Si matrix (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003).

### Modern SDD-EDS Precision and Repeatability

Newbury and Ritchie (J. Mater. Sci. 50, 493–518, 2015; DOI: 10.1007/s10853-014-8685-2) demonstrated that SDD-EDS with standards-based k-ratio analysis and NIST DTSA-II can match WDS precision and accuracy. On NIST SRM 470 (K411 glass), 20 randomly selected polished locations gave single-measurement relative standard deviations of 0.079% for Si (25.4 wt%), 0.11% for Mg (8.9 wt%), 0.089% for Ca (11.1 wt%), and 0.26% for Fe (11.2 wt%), with mean relative errors below 1.8% (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007). For NIST SRM 483 (Fe–3Si steel), Si at 3.22 wt% was measured at 3.13 wt% with 0.24% replicate relative precision over nine replicates (pqac-00000010). Across 50 major/minor elemental determinations, 56% of relative deviations were within ±1% and 84% within ±2% (pqac-00000011). Detection limits below 0.001 mass fraction (1000 ppm) were achieved within 500-second acquisitions (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000012). Spectra with approximately 1.5 × 10⁶ total counts yielded RSDs below 1–2% for oxides above 10 wt% and below 2% for most components between 1 and 10 wt% (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003).

### Do Counting Statistics Dominate?

At 5–6 wt% Si, counting statistics are emphatically not the limiting factor for a standards-based measurement on a polished bulk specimen. With 10⁴–10⁵ net Si Kα counts, counting precision contributes less than ±0.1 wt% per measurement. The NPL measurement-uncertainty guide (Tong and Mingard, 2026; DOI: 10.47120/npl.mat135) identifies matrix-correction model uncertainty (approximately 1–7% relative for standards-based methods), specimen geometry and surface preparation, detector-efficiency calibration (especially below 2 keV), and beam-current stability (verified at 0.2% in a controlled test) as non-counting error sources that collectively dominate the uncertainty budget for major constituents (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000055).

---

## (2) Unpolished Loose Particles versus Polished Cross-Sections

### Particle Geometry Effects

The standards-based k-ratio protocol assumes both the unknown and standard are flat, polished, bulk targets at defined angles to the beam and detector. For spherical powder particles, three geometry-dependent effects alter Si Kα intensities relative to a bulk flat specimen:

**Mass effect:** Electrons scatter out through the sides and bottom of small particles, reducing X-ray generation. At 25 kV, Small (J. Res. NIST 107, 555, 2002; DOI: 10.6028/jres.107.047) measured approximately 50% intensity loss for 2 µm glass microspheres and 75% for approximately 1 µm particles. At 15 kV, the maximum loss fell to approximately 13% for a 1.8 µm sphere. At 10 kV, the loss was generally limited to about 10%, with particle/bulk ratios remaining near unity from approximately 0.9–18 µm (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000076).

**Absorption effect:** Si Kα photons (1.74 keV) are strongly absorbed by aluminum (just above the Al K-edge at 1.56 keV). In a spherical particle, the shorter average escape path length relative to a bulk specimen reduces self-absorption, causing the apparent Si Kα intensity to increase. At 25 kV, Si particle/bulk ratios reached approximately 1.4 and Mg ratios approximately 1.6 for microspheres larger than about 4 µm. These effects were substantially reduced at 15 kV and relatively flat at 10 kV (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000076, pqac-00000077).

**Combined geometry errors:** Newbury and Ritchie (SPIE 8036, 803602, 2011; DOI: 10.1117/12.881040) showed that all tested non-ideal geometries—scratches, fracture surfaces, chips, shards, and particles—produced strong deviations from the true composition, with errors up to a factor of ten compared with flat polished material. Normalized elemental errors remained within approximately 20% of the correct values only when the raw analytical total fell between 80% and 120% (pqac-00000014). The raw analytical total (expected near 98–102% for a fully characterized specimen) is the primary diagnostic: normalization to 100% conceals these geometry-induced errors rather than correcting them (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017).

### Normalization and Peak-to-Background Methods

The peak-to-background (P/B) ratio method exploits the approximate invariance of the characteristic-to-continuum intensity ratio between particle and bulk specimens of identical composition. The measured particle peak is normalized by the local continuum to produce a geometry-corrected, bulk-equivalent intensity (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000026). Earlier implementations commonly achieved about 10–20% relative error for micron-scale particles (pqac-00000028). A modern automated P/B workflow (Giunto et al., Nat. Commun. 17, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76633-x) validated on 74 single-phase powder samples achieved relative deviations generally within 5–10% of expected compositions on raw, irregularly shaped particles without embedding or polishing, using only one experimental standard per element. This is comparable to standardless analysis on polished bulk but weaker than standards-based analysis on a well-prepared flat mount (approximately 2–5% relative) (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000071). The method incorporates corrections for continuum-generation differences (Zc, which can vary 20–500% between particle and standard as a function of average atomic number), absorption (Ac), backscattering (Rc), fluorescence (Fc), and a geometric absorption-path modification with fitted parameters z₀ and m (pqac-00000022).

### Recommended Particle Size Relative to Interaction Volume

At 5 kV, the electron interaction and X-ray generation volumes are much smaller than at 20 kV; for microspheres above about 1–2 µm, the particle effectively behaves as a bulk specimen. At 10 kV, particles larger than approximately 1.4 µm gave particle/bulk values within 0.9–1.1 for all elements in K411 glass, though the irregular-shard variation was approximately 8–12% relative. At 15 kV, mass effects only approached unity for particles larger than approximately 3 µm. At 20–25 kV, particles must exceed 5 µm to approach bulk behavior for high-energy lines (pqac-00000072, pqac-00000074, pqac-00000075, pqac-00000077, pqac-00000078). However, at 5 kV a contamination layer as thin as 5 nm of carbon reduced Ca k-ratios by 7%, and 10 nm reduced them by 13%, making low-overvoltage elements vulnerable (pqac-00000075). Thus, **10 kV represents a practical optimum** for particle analysis of Al–Si, offering low geometric errors while maintaining adequate overvoltage for Si Kα (overvoltage ratio ≈ 5.8).

---

## (3) Within-Particle Microstructural Heterogeneity

### Rapidly Solidified Al–Si Microstructure

Gas-atomized hypoeutectic Al–Si droplets solidify rapidly and develop highly heterogeneous microstructures within individual particles. Trivedi et al. (Acta Mater. 51, 289–300, 2003; DOI: 10.1016/s1359-6454(02)00226-4) demonstrated that latent-heat release produces recalescence, causing non-steady growth conditions during solidification of a single droplet, so that the interface velocity, thermal gradient, and cooling rate change from the nucleation site inward (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035). Genau (OSTI 835374, 2004; DOI: 10.2172/835374) showed that Al–3Si and Al–6Si particles in the sub-micrometer to tens-of-micrometer range commonly exhibited three successive microstructural regions: an initial supersaturated α-Al solid solution formed under planar growth, followed by a segregate-free zone during recalescence, then breakdown to a cellular structure with increasing Si partitioning (pqac-00000029).

### Dendrite Arm Spacing and Si Distribution

For gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, Vanzetti et al. (Metals 13, 1845, 2023; DOI: 10.3390/met13111845) reported a mean secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) of 2.19 ± 0.56 µm, with Si concentrated in the interdendritic eutectic network while the α-Al dendrite cores were Si-depleted (pqac-00000059). Albu et al. (Addit. Manuf. 36, 101605, 2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101605) found that eutectic Si in AlSi10Mg powder consisted of crystalline nanoparticles approximately 5–30 nm in size, with some amorphous Si nanoparticles (5–10 nm) embedded in the α-Al matrix (pqac-00000060).

### Implications for Raster Size

A spot analysis placed on an α-Al cell will return a Si concentration far below the bulk particle mean, while a spot on eutectic Si will return a value far above it. To obtain a representative per-particle composition, the raster or summed area must span at least 5–10 SDAS lengths—approximately 10–20 µm for AlSi10Mg—and should ideally cover the entire particle cross-section on a polished mount. For particles in the 20–60 µm size range typical of atomized powder, a whole-cross-section raster on a polished section is feasible and strongly recommended. On loose particles, this corresponds to an area scan covering most of the visible particle face; for particles smaller than about 10 µm, the entire particle may fall within or near the interaction volume at 10–15 kV, effectively producing an area-averaged composition by default, though with attendant geometry-effect artifacts.

---

## (4) Sampling Statistics: Number of Particles and Size-Composition Correlations

### Particle-to-Particle Scatter

Individual atomized particles can differ in composition due to heterogeneous nucleation, stochastic cooling histories, and variable solute trapping. Genau (2004) documented that smaller particles are more likely to form supersaturated solid solution with suppressed segregation, while larger particles develop primary Si crystals and coarser eutectic structures (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000065, pqac-00000067). No universal particle-to-particle standard deviation for Si in atomized Al–Si has been published. In the Giunto et al. (2026) automated EDS framework, 48.1% of elemental measurements across 74 diverse powder samples had standard deviations below 1 at% and 91.2% below 2 at%, but these values cover many chemistries and are not specific to atomized Al–Si (pqac-00000071).

### How Many Particles Per Lot?

For a two-sample t-test comparing lot means, the required number of particles per lot is n ≥ 2(z_α/2 + z_β)² × s_p² / Δ², where s_p is the between-particle standard deviation, Δ is the target difference (1 wt%), and z values correspond to the desired confidence (1.96 for 95%) and power (0.84 for 80%). If s_p = 1.0 wt% Si, approximately n ≈ 16 particles per lot provide 80% power; if s_p = 2.0 wt%, approximately n ≈ 63 are needed. Because s_p is unknown a priori, a pilot study of at least 30 particles per lot is advisable to estimate it. In practice, 50–100 particles per lot is a conservative and achievable target with automated SEM-EDS.

### Composition–Size Correlations

Published AlSi10Mg powders showed nominal differences in Si between fine and coarse fractions: Balbaa et al. (Addit. Manuf. 37, 101630, 2021; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101630) reported 8.56 wt% Si for the fine fraction versus 9.76 wt% Si for the coarse fraction, though these were nominal compositions rather than direct measurements of atomization-induced segregation (pqac-00000069). Genau (2004) established the physical basis: fine droplets cool faster, undercool more, and trap more solute into supersaturated α-Al, while coarse droplets solidify more slowly with greater equilibrium partitioning and Si-rich second-phase formation (pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065, pqac-00000068). Thus, a real composition–size correlation is physically expected, though its magnitude for a specific atomization run must be measured empirically.

### Segregation in Containers and Sampling

Powder in a collection jar can undergo size segregation due to vibration, sifting, and funnel flow. Neikov and Yefimov (Handbook of Non-Ferrous Metal Powders, 3–62, 2019; DOI: 10.1016/b978-0-08-100543-9.00001-4) documented that funnel-flow conditions create stagnant peripheral zones and increased sifting segregation, while vibration drives fine particles downward and coarse particles upward (or vice versa depending on density and morphology) (pqac-00000040). If fine particles are enriched in the bottom of the jar and coarse particles near the top (or the reverse), and if Si differs by particle size as described above, then a top-versus-bottom sampling without size matching will produce an apparent composition difference that reflects size segregation rather than incomplete melt mixing.

The reliability of sample-splitting methods varies dramatically: quartering produces standard deviations of approximately 6.81%, scoop sampling 5.14%, chute splitting 1.01%, and rotary sample division only 0.146% (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039). **Rotary division is essential** for any quantitative comparison at the 1 wt% level. Multiple increments should be taken from at least 300 mm below the surface of each jar stratum (pqac-00000037).

---

## (5) Published Examples: EDS/EPMA versus Bulk Methods

### Particle-Level EDS on Powder

The most comprehensive published validation of quantitative SEM-EDS on raw powder is by Giunto et al. (Nat. Commun. 17, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76633-x), who demonstrated their automated P/B workflow on 74 single-phase powder samples spanning 38 elements. Overall relative deviations were within 5–10% for most elements, with 75.8% of cluster-centroid compositions within 5% and 93.6% within 10% relative deviation (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000071). For multiphase and powder-mixture samples, k-means clustering resolved individual phase compositions and minority phases (pqac-00000047). However, this work did not specifically benchmark against ICP-OES or XRF on the same sample splits.

### ICP-MS Composition of Gas-Atomized Al–Si

Vanzetti et al. (Metals 13, 1845, 2023; DOI: 10.3390/met13111845) reported ICP-MS chemical compositions for AlSi10Mg-based gas-atomized powders with notable scatter: the base AlSi10Mg alloy measured Si = 11.94 ± 1.96 wt% and Mg = 0.54 ± 0.33 wt% by ICP-MS on five unsieved samples (pqac-00000062). The large standard deviations likely reflect real particle-to-particle or subsample-to-subsample variation rather than ICP-MS instrument imprecision, since bulk ICP-OES for dissolved metals typically achieves 0.2–0.5 wt% resolution (pqac-00000046). EDS compositional mapping on the same powders confirmed Si in the eutectic network and Cu in interdendritic θ-phase channels, consistent with the ICP-MS bulk values, but no quantitative EDS–ICP comparison was presented (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059).

### Nickel-Based Alloy 625 Powder

Mostafaei et al. (Powder Technol. 333, 180–192, 2018; DOI: 10.1016/j.powtec.2018.04.014) compared gas-atomized and water-atomized alloy 625 powders using SEM-EDS, reporting that gas-atomized powder had composition closer to nominal. However, their compositional assessment relied on manufacturer-reported values and did not provide a rigorous EDS-versus-ICP validation (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043).

### Where the Literature Is Silent

**Direct same-split EDS-versus-ICP or EDS-versus-XRF validation studies on atomized Al–Si powder are sparse to nonexistent.** Most published powder-characterization work reports EDS results alongside manufacturer-specified or separately measured bulk compositions, without presenting paired analytical comparisons on identically prepared splits. Similarly, no published study could be identified that specifically tested whether SEM-EDS on atomized Al–Si powder can reliably detect a 1 wt% Si difference between lots at a stated confidence level. The statistical framework for particle counting (how many particles, how to account for particle-to-particle scatter, hierarchical variance decomposition) is largely absent from the powder-metallurgy EDS literature and must be imported from environmental particle analysis, mineral liberation analysis, or clinical assay-validation frameworks.

The accuracy of XRD lattice-parameter or phase-fraction measurements for quantifying Si in rapidly solidified Al–Si is limited by the fact that conventional XRD phase sensitivity is commonly several volume percent and cannot directly recover Si retained in supersaturated α-Al solid solution (pqac-00000041).

---

## Synthesis and Recommendations

The table below summarizes a recommended experimental protocol for resolving a 1 wt% Si difference between two powder lots at 95% confidence.

| Protocol element | Recommendation | Rationale / literature support |
|---|---|---|
| Specimen preparation | **Primary method:** Embed each independently split subsample in low-viscosity epoxy, vacuum-impregnate, grind, and polish through particle equators to a flat finish. Carbon-coat mounts and standards similarly. Randomize fields and exclude particles intersecting mount edges or pores. Use loose particles only for screening or when polishing is impossible. | Standards-based EDS assumes flat bulk geometry. Polished standards produced approximately 0.08–0.26% relative single-measurement precision and about 0.2% spatial RSD for Si, whereas scratches, shards, and particles generated broad errors approaching an order of magnitude. Normalization to 100% can hide these errors (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000017). |
| Accelerating voltage | For polished Al–Si sections, begin at **10 kV** and verify the result at **15 kV** on a subset. Use 15–20 kV only when particles are comfortably larger than the interaction volume and additional count rate is needed. For loose particles, prefer **10 kV** and particles larger than approximately 3–5 µm; 5 kV may reduce geometry effects further but is more sensitive to contamination and low overvoltage. | At 10 kV, approximately 0.9–18 µm glass spheres generally gave particle-to-bulk ratios within 0.9–1.1 above about 1.4 µm. At 15 kV, a 1.8 µm sphere lost about 13% intensity; at 25 kV, 1–2 µm spheres lost 50–75%, and Si Kα particle-to-bulk ratios reached about 1.4. Ten kilovolts gave the lowest variation for irregular shards; 5 kV suffered contamination-related bias (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000072, pqac-00000075, pqac-00000077). |
| Spectrum acquisition | Acquire **at least 10,000 background-corrected Si Kα counts per accepted particle mean**; 20,000–50,000 is preferable when time permits. Keep detector dead time near **10% and below 15%**, monitor beam current with a Faraday cup or reference standard, bracket each session with a homogeneous Al–Si control, and use identical conditions for standards and unknowns. Determine live time empirically from the Si count rate. | Ten thousand net counts limit ideal Poisson relative uncertainty to about 1%, or approximately 0.05–0.06 wt% at 5–6 wt% Si. High-count SDD spectra readily achieve sub-percent repeatability, so geometry, microstructure, and sampling—not counting statistics—should dominate. Excess dead time increases coincidence artifacts; stable beam dose is required for rigorous k-ratios (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000057). |
| Quantification | Use the existing **standards-based k-ratio/DTSA-II** procedure with pure Al and Si standards and matched beam conditions; retain both normalized composition and the **raw analytical total**. If available, analyze an Al–Si reference alloy near 5–6 wt% Si as independent QC. For loose particles, use a validated **peak-to-local-background method** with particle filtering rather than ordinary bulk ZAF alone. | DTSA-II standards-based analysis placed 84% of 50 major/minor determinations within ±2% relative of reference values. Raw totals near 98–102% are a useful geometry diagnostic; normalization alone can conceal anomalous absorption. Modified P/B methods reduce finite-size and topographic effects but generally retain about 5–10% relative error on raw particles, versus roughly 2–5% for well-prepared standards or polished specimens (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000044). |
| Per-particle raster or area | On polished sections, raster nearly the **entire exposed particle cross-section**, remaining at least one interaction radius from epoxy and neighboring particles. If whole-section rastering is impractical, combine systematically distributed fields whose total span covers at least **5–10 dendrite or cell spacings**—approximately **10–20 µm** for an AlSi10Mg-like spacing of 2.19 µm—and include the particle center and rim. Do not use one arbitrary point as the particle mean. | Rapidly solidified Al–Si particles contain α-Al cells or dendrites, Si-rich interdendritic eutectic, supersaturated Al, and nanoscale Si. Morphology and spacing can change across one droplet. Reported AlSi10Mg secondary dendrite-arm spacing was 2.19 ± 0.56 µm, while Si was concentrated in interdendritic networks (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000065). |
| Number of particles per lot | Analyze an initial **30 randomly selected particles per lot**, then estimate between-particle SD, `s_p`, from per-particle means. For two equal-sized independent lots, use at minimum `n ≥ 2(1.96s_p/1.0)²` particles per lot for a 95% CI on a 1 wt% difference; for 80% power use `n ≥ 2(1.96 + 0.84)²s_p²`. The confidence criterion gives approximately **8, 18, and 31 particles per lot** for `s_p = 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 wt%`, respectively. In practice, use **at least 30 and preferably 50–100 particles per lot**. Treat particles—not spectra or spots—as independent replicates. | Published powder studies support averaging many spectra but do not provide a universal particle count for atomized Al–Si. Automated powder EDS showed that cluster averaging improved agreement with expected composition, while real particle-to-particle variance depends on particle size, nucleation, and solute trapping. Sample size must therefore be calculated from observed particle variance rather than X-ray counts (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000071). |
| Powder sampling and splitting | Treat top, middle, and bottom as three separately collected strata. Take several increments across each stratum, combine them, gently homogenize without grinding, and reduce each composite with a **rotary sample divider** or validated multi-chute riffle splitter. Prepare at least **two independent splits and mounts per stratum**; do not scoop the analytical portion directly from the jar. | Reported subdivision variability was about 0.146% for rotary division and 1.01% for chute splitting, compared with 5.14% for scoop sampling and 6.81% for quartering. Vibration, funnel flow, and sifting can produce vertical size segregation in stored powder (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040). |
| Particle-size stratification | Measure every analyzed particle’s equivalent diameter and assign predefined size bins. Compare lots both **within common size bins** and after reweighting to a common particle-size distribution. Also sieve representative bulk splits and analyze at least fine, middle, and coarse fractions independently. Include size and a lot-by-size interaction in the statistical model. | Fine droplets cool faster, undercool more, and exhibit greater solute trapping and less segregation; coarse droplets more readily form segregated structures. Published fine and coarse AlSi10Mg powders differed nominally in Si—8.56 versus 9.76 wt%—although this alone does not prove atomization segregation. Jar size segregation can therefore mimic a top-to-bottom Si gradient (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000068, pqac-00000069). |
| Statistical comparison | Fit a hierarchical model or mixed-effects ANOVA with **jar stratum or lot as the fixed effect**, size bin as a covariate, and split, mount, and particle as nested random effects. Report the top-minus-bottom estimate with its 95% CI, variance components, rejected-spectrum fraction, and sensitivity analysis with and without size adjustment. Claim resolution only when the 95% CI excludes zero and is sufficiently narrow to distinguish the specified 1 wt% contrast. | Repeated spectra on one particle improve counting precision but do not increase the number of independently sampled particles. Separating analytical repeatability, within-particle variation, between-particle variation, and split-to-split sampling variance prevents pseudoreplication and distinguishes a chemical gradient from particle-size segregation. |
| Confirmation by bulk method | Digest independent rotary-divided splits from every stratum and measure Si by **ICP-OES or ICP-MS**; alternatively, use calibrated bulk XRF. Run duplicate preparations, blanks, spikes, and a certified Al-alloy reference. Use XRD lattice parameter or phase fractions only as supporting evidence—not as the primary 1 wt% Si assay. Agreement between size-adjusted particle EDS and bulk chemistry is the strongest evidence of incomplete melt mixing. | EDS provides particle-resolved heterogeneity, whereas ICP and XRF provide mass-weighted bulk composition. Published gas-atomized Al–Si–Cu–Mg work used ICP-MS for post-atomization bulk chemistry and EDS/XRD for phase-scale segregation; direct same-split EDS-versus-ICP validation of atomized Al–Si powder remains sparse. Conventional XRD phase sensitivity is commonly several volume percent and cannot directly recover Si retained in supersaturated α-Al (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000062). |


*Table: A quantitative protocol for distinguishing powder lots differing by 1 wt% Si while controlling counting, geometry, microstructure, particle-size, and bulk-sampling uncertainties.*

### Key Conclusions

1. **Counting statistics are not the bottleneck.** With modern SDD-EDS, accumulating ≥10,000 net Si Kα counts per particle takes seconds, yielding counting precision well below ±0.1 wt% (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000010).

2. **Particle geometry is the largest single analytical error source for loose particles.** Without correction, Si Kα k-ratios from unpolished spheres can be biased by 10–40% relative at 15–25 kV due to mass and absorption effects, especially for the strong Al K-edge absorption of Si Kα at 1.74 keV (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000014). Polished cross-sections eliminate this problem; P/B methods reduce it to approximately 5–10% relative (pqac-00000044).

3. **Within-particle microstructural heterogeneity demands area-averaging.** With SDAS approximately 2 µm and Si concentrated in the eutectic network, spot analyses are not representative. Whole-cross-section rastering on polished mounts is optimal (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060).

4. **Particle-to-particle scatter and particle-size-dependent composition are the dominant sources of between-lot variance.** The required number of particles depends on this scatter, which must be measured empirically; 50–100 particles per lot is a practical starting point (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000069).

5. **Physical sampling is critical.** Rotary sample division (0.146% SD) rather than scooping (5.14% SD) or quartering (6.81% SD) is essential. Size segregation in the collection jar can create spurious top-versus-bottom composition gradients that mimic incomplete mixing (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000040).

6. **Confirmation by ICP-OES or bulk XRF on independent splits is strongly recommended**, as no published validation has demonstrated that particle-level SEM-EDS alone can reliably resolve a 1 wt% Si difference in atomized Al–Si at 95% confidence.

In summary, the measurement is feasible but requires careful control of specimen preparation (polished sections preferred), beam voltage (10 kV for loose particles, 10–15 kV for polished sections), sufficient particle counts (≥50 per lot), proper powder sampling (rotary splitting), particle-size stratification, and independent bulk-chemistry confirmation. The dominant challenge is not counting statistics but rather the interplay of particle geometry artifacts, microstructural heterogeneity, particle-to-particle compositional scatter, and physical sampling bias.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general counting-statistics relationships relevant to estimating analytical sensitivity in electron-microprobe analysis, but it does not state Ziebold’s specific result or give a direct number of counts required for 1 wt% precision. Detection limit is evaluated using a 3-sigma criterion, with the minimum detectable concentration depending on background intensity, background counting time, standard intensity and concentration, and relative probe currents. The detection limit decreases with the square root of the peak-to-background ratio, net peak counting rate, and counting time; therefore, increasing any one of these parameters by a factor of four reduces the detection limit by a factor of two. Higher beam current and, for many elements, higher accelerating voltage increase characteristic X-ray intensity and improve sensitivity. For precise low-concentration measurements, the excerpt reports that high probe current combined with long counting times may be necessary, citing 180 seconds or more for Zn near 56 ppm in olivine. It also notes that dividing long measurements into shorter peak and background intervals can reduce instrumental drift, while equal peak and background counting times maximize precision in the background-corrected intensity. These principles can support a Poisson-counting estimate, but the requested 1 wt% precision count requirement is not explicitly provided here.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses EDS counting statistics, sensitivity, and detection limits, but it does not specifically cite Ziebold or state the number of counts required for 1 wt% precision. It recommends collecting spectra with approximately 10^7 integrated counts for accurate low-level quantification, while noting that SDD-EDS can produce spectra exceeding 50 million counts in practical counting times. Such high counts lower the minimum detectable concentration to substantially below 0.001 mass fraction (1000 ppm). The excerpt also gives a concentration-limit-of-detection relationship involving the background counts (NB), the measured peak intensity (NS), and the known concentration of a standard (CS): CDL = 3 sqrt(NB)/(NS − NB) × CS. For ideal Poisson counting of a net peak, relative statistical uncertainty scales approximately as 1/sqrt(N), so a 1% counting-statistical precision would conventionally correspond to roughly 10,000 net counts; however, that numerical inference is not explicitly stated in this excerpt and practical EDS precision also depends on background, overlaps, deadtime, matrix corrections, and calibration.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents high-precision, standards-based quantitative SDD-EDS analysis using NIST DTSA-II. Measurements were acquired at 20 keV for 50 seconds, yielding approximately 5 million counts, and processed with multiple linear least-squares peak fitting. Pure Mg, Si, and Fe standards and NIST SRM 470 glass as the Ca standard were used to measure intensities and form k-values; concentrations were then calculated using the XPP matrix-correction procedure in DTSA-II. For 20 randomly selected locations on polished NIST SRM 470 (K411 glass), measured averages agreed with certified SRM values within 1.7% relative. The reported single-measurement relative standard deviations were approximately 0.11% for Mg, 0.079% for Si, 0.089% for Ca, and 0.26% for Fe, while 20-location relative standard deviations were 0.5%, 0.21%, 0.23%, and 0.275%, respectively. The paper defines major constituents as above 10 weight percent and minor constituents as between 1 and 10 weight percent. It emphasizes that this accuracy and repeatability apply to the ideal polished bulk geometry; rough, irregular, or particle specimens can compromise standards-based k-ratio quantification.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a standards-based EDS quantitative-analysis workflow relevant to evaluating accuracy and repeatability for major and minor constituents. Spectra were acquired using vendor EDS software, exported in the Microscopy Society of America .msa format, and processed with NIST DTSA-II. DTSA-II uses multiple linear least-squares peak fitting with measured reference spectra, preferably from pure elements or stable stoichiometric compounds for beam-sensitive or vacuum-incompatible elements. Measured k-ratios are converted to concentration ratios using Pouchou–Pichoir matrix corrections for electron retardation, backscattering, self-absorption, and secondary fluorescence. The study used NIST certified microanalysis standards with bulk composition and micrometer-scale homogeneity, along with stoichiometric compounds and prepared microprobe standards. The raw analytical total is an important quality-control indicator: at 10–20 keV it generally ranged from 0.98 to 1.02, while totals below unity may signal an unrecognized constituent. After checking the constituents and deviations, concentrations may be normalized to unity. The excerpt also notes that direct oxygen determination produced relative deviations of 3.2% and 1.7% in two glasses, both within ±5%. It explicitly frames the broader study as comparing EDS k-ratio precision with WDS and assessing analytical accuracy and detection limits, although SDD-specific hardware performance is not identified here.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly supports the use of SDD-EDS for quantitative elemental microanalysis with precision and accuracy potentially comparable to WDS. Its high throughput, spectral resolution, and stability allow high-count spectra to be collected, improving peak-fitting performance when severe overlaps occur. The authors report accurate analyses for major/minor and trace-element interference cases, including situations in which a major constituent overlaps a minor or trace constituent. Low-atomic-number elements such as C, N, O, and F can also be analyzed accurately, and trace constituents below 0.001 mass fraction (1000 ppm) may be detected within approximately 500 seconds. For standards-based quantitative analysis, the Castaing k-ratio protocol measures the same characteristic X-ray peak in an unknown and a compositionally appropriate standard under identical beam energy, dose, and detector conditions. The ratio cancels common detector-efficiency effects. Concentrations are then obtained using matrix corrections represented by Z, A, F, and c, accounting for atomic-number effects, absorption, and secondary fluorescence or continuum contributions. The excerpt states that standards need not closely match the unknown and may include pure elements or suitable stoichiometric compounds. It does not specifically discuss repeatability statistics for SDD-EDS or implementation details of NIST DTSA-II.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes quantitative SEM/SDD-EDS performance when measurements follow a standards-based k-ratio protocol with matrix correction, rather than relying on standardless normalization. Reported accuracy is routinely within ±5% relative for major constituents (mass fraction above 0.1), approximately ±10% for minor constituents (0.01–0.1), and ±25% for trace constituents (0.001–0.01). Detection limits can reach approximately 0.0005 mass fraction for many elements. Tables 13–16 demonstrate repeatability and agreement with ideal stoichiometry for carbides, nitrides, oxides, and fluorides; replicate scatter values (r) are generally small, supporting high precision under controlled conditions. Table 17 reports NIST K497 glass detection limits from 41–329 ppm for selected elements under a 500-second acquisition, with uncertainties listed for each CDL. Achieving EPMA/WDS-level results requires careful measurement science, including polished unknowns and standards with surface relief below 50 nm rms. The excerpt emphasizes that specimen topography, local inclination, and thickness can cause severe quantitative errors. In the pyrite example analyzed with DTSA-II, k-ratio and matrix-correction results provide a warning through the raw analytical total, whereas standardless analysis can conceal topographic problems. Thus, repeatability and accuracy claims apply primarily to flat, properly prepared specimens measured with standards-based k-ratio analysis.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents standards-based SEM/SDD-EDS k-ratio analysis as capable of high accuracy when the measurement science procedures developed for EPMA/WDS are rigorously followed. Unknowns and standards must be measured under reproducible beam energy, electron dose, detector live time, energy resolution, geometry, and specimen tilt conditions. A Faraday cup and digital picoammeter are identified as necessary for a fully rigorous k-ratio protocol. The authors recommend controlling beam current so detector deadtime is approximately 10%, which minimizes coincidence or sum peaks; deadtime above about 15% increasingly worsens this problem. Repeatability is supported by SDD stability, allowing archived standard spectra to be reused when quality assurance confirms that current conditions match the original measurements. Standards may be pure elements, stoichiometric compounds, or homogeneous alloys, glasses, and minerals with accurately known compositions. Table 5 reports small relative errors for sulfide analyses at 20 keV, generally from 0 to 3.6% for sulfur and 0 to 1.4% for the metal component. High-count spectra with stable peak shape and position support statistically robust MLLS peak fitting, including severe overlaps. Using NIST DTSA-II, SDD-EDS was demonstrated to match WDS performance for k-ratio determination in difficult Ba–Ti spectral interference cases.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides quantitative SDD-EDS performance data from NIST DTSA-II analyses, including standards-based measurements, estimated combined uncertainties, relative deviations (RDEV), and repeatability from multiple replicate measurements. For NIST SRM 483 Fe–3Si steel analyzed at 20 keV using pure-element standards and K-shell x-rays, Si was measured at 0.0313 versus the certified 0.0322, with a combined uncertainty of ±0.0001, an RDEV of −2.8%, and nine-replicate relative precision of 0.24%; Fe was measured at 0.9687 with ±0.0019 uncertainty and 0.02% replicate variation. SRM 2062 Al–Ti–Nb–W, also analyzed with pure-element standards at 20 keV, showed RDEVs from −1.8% to 2.3% and replicate precision from 0.14% to 2.5%, with the poorest repeatability for the minor W component. Glass SRM 470 results at 10 keV illustrate the effect of oxygen treatment: using assumed stoichiometry, major-element RDEVs ranged from −0.4% to 3.1% with nine-replicate precision of 0.04–0.27%; direct MgO-based oxygen analysis produced oxygen RDEV of 3.2% and ±0.0046 uncertainty. These tables support assessment of accuracy against certified standards and precision for both major and minor elements.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents SEM/SDD-EDS quantitative performance using a standards-based k-ratio protocol and NIST DTSA-II on NIST SRM 470 (K411 glass). Under ideal specimen conditions—a flat, highly polished bulk surface with a thin conductive carbon coating—20 randomly selected analyses produced a narrow distribution for Mg and Fe, supporting good repeatability. Table 3 reports the certified values, mean EDS results, standard deviations, and relative errors: O was 0.424 certified versus 0.428 measured, with 0.022 SD and 0.9% relative error; Mg 0.0885 versus 0.0876, SD 0.045 and −1.1%; Si 0.254 versus 0.258, SD 0.053 and 1.6%; Ca 0.111 versus 0.111, SD 0.026 and 0%; and Fe 0.112 versus 0.114, SD 0.031 and 1.8%. Geometric effects produce a wider error range than in polished specimens, and anomalous absorption—especially at low photon energies—can make conventional k-ratio and matrix corrections followed by normalization produce unacceptably large errors. contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses geometric and absorption effects for irregular specimens, including microscopic particles. In a spherical or otherwise curved particle, the local surface curvature can shorten the X-ray escape path relative to an ideal flat polished bulk specimen. This reduces absorption and preferentially enhances the measured intensity of low-energy photons, potentially distorting k-ratios and calculated concentrations. Conversely, locations such as the bottoms of holes can increase the absorption path and selectively suppress low-energy photons. The study reports that all tested non-ideal geometries produced strong deviations from the true composition; errors could be a factor of ten or more compared with flat bulk material, making quantitative results unreliable for many practical comparisons. The excerpt does not separately quantify mass-effect, fluorescence-effect, or peak-to-background contributions, but it demonstrates that geometry-driven absorption changes substantially affect apparent composition. It also warns that normalization can conceal these errors. A recommended diagnostic is to retain the raw, un-normalized analytical total: when all relevant elements are measured, a sound k-value analysis should generally total 98–102%. Totals outside this range indicate factors such as geometric effects. For totals between 80% and 120%, normalized elemental errors were reported to remain within about 20% of the correct values, providing an indication—not a correction—of the broadened uncertainty.

Departures from this geometry—such as those expected for spherical or otherwise unpolished particles—can produce very large changes in measured X-ray intensities, with particularly important consequences when low- and high-energy photons are analyzed together. Standardless calculations require concentrations to be internally normalized to exactly 100% because the relationship between electron dose, absolute detector efficiency, and remote standards is lost; this normalization can conceal missing constituents and create a false impression of accuracy. By contrast, standards-based analyses generally produce totals near, but not exactly, unity (typically 0.98–1.02), and deviations can provide diagnostic information, such as unrecognized oxygen or uncontrolled differences in coatings, oxides, or specimen geometry.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses geometric particle effects in X-ray microanalysis of spherical microspheres, particularly the particle mass and particle absorption effects as functions of particle diameter and accelerating voltage. At 25 kV, electron scattering out of the bottom and sides of small spheres produces substantial mass-effect losses: approximately 50% loss for a 2 µm sphere and 75% for the smallest, roughly 1 µm particles. At 15 kV, the maximum loss falls to about 13% for a 1.8 µm sphere, while at 10 kV the loss is generally limited to about 10%, with particle/bulk ratios remaining near unity from 0.9 to 18 µm except for an anomalous Fe result. For low-energy Si Kα (1.74 keV) and Mg Kα (1.24 keV) lines, absorption becomes important, especially for particles larger than approximately 4 µm. At 25 kV, Mg particle/bulk ratios reach about 1.6 and Si ratios about 1.4; these effects are reduced at 15 kV and become comparatively flat at 10 kV. contexts.context: The excerpt provides experimental evidence that specimen geometry strongly affects SEM/EDS quantitative analysis when compared with an ideal flat, polished bulk specimen. K411 glass was analyzed in several forms: polished bulk material, surface voids remaining after polishing, macroscopic fracture chips, and microscopic milled shards. Fixed-beam measurements were made at different locations, including approximately the center of microscopic particles; a second strategy used a continuous bracketing or overscan field around the particle. The plotted Fe–Mg results show that these geometries produce different normalized compositions and greater scatter than bulk measurements, demonstrating that unpolished surfaces, holes, chips, and small particles can generate systematic errors. The discussion attributes the differences primarily to mass/overvoltage and absorption effects. Mg K photons are low energy (1.254 keV), whereas Fe Kα is much higher energy (6.400 keV), so their intensities respond differently to geometry. Higher-energy lines are more affected by changes in electron backscattering and beam penetration, while low-energy photons are more strongly absorbed and therefore sensitive to the escape path length. A beam at the bottom of a void can have a longer path and enhanced absorption, whereas a reduced escape path can increase low-energy intensity. contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses geometry-related limitations of the peak-to-background (P/B) method for quantitative EDS. It states that using the ratio of the characteristic peak area to the immediately underlying background makes the measurement relatively insensitive to small changes in surface geometry. This suggests that modest roughness or geometric variation may be partly compensated because geometry affects peak and background in similar ways and therefore tends to cancel in the ratio. However, the method is not immune to severe surface artifacts: the sample should be made as smooth as practicable, since uneven fracture faces can produce unreliable X-ray results through preferential masking and absorption. The excerpt therefore supports using P/B measurements for particles or irregular specimens only when geometric irregularities are limited and do not strongly shadow or absorb emitted X-rays. It also cites foundational work by Statham and Pawley on particle microanalysis using peak-to-background measurements, and by Small et al. on quantitative analysis of single particles. The passage does not provide a detailed correction algorithm for large roughness, particle shape, tilt, shadowing, or absorption; instead, it emphasizes minimizing these artifacts through specimen preparation and recognizing the method’s practical geometry tolerance.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly describes the peak-to-background (P/B) ratio method for quantitative EDS analysis of particles and rough, non-bulk geometries. Conventional EDS assumes a flat bulk sample that fully contains the X-ray generation volume, whereas loose particles introduce geometry-dependent effects. The P/B approach compensates for these effects by exploiting the approximate invariance of the peak-to-background ratio between particle and bulk samples of identical composition. Particle peak and background intensities are measured, and the particle peak intensity is transformed into a geometry-corrected, bulk-equivalent intensity suitable for conventional quantification models. The method therefore addresses geometry artifacts arising from particle shape, finite size, absorption, and substrate-related effects. The implementation described here improves background modeling by accounting for continuum generation, absorption, backscattering, detector response, and geometry-dependent X-ray path lengths. It also incorporates electron stopping-power effects when estimating the bulk reference background, reducing errors when the standard and unknown sample have substantially different average atomic numbers. These corrections allow a single experimental standard per element to be used across samples with widely varying compositions. The excerpt does not explicitly identify Statham and Small by name, but it presents the relevant conceptual basis and refinements of the P/B method for particle-level quantitative EDS.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a peak-to-background (P/B) approach for quantitative SEM-EDS analysis and identifies corrections especially relevant to particles and rough or irregular surfaces. Elemental mass fractions are calculated by comparing the characteristic peak-to-background ratio from a particle with that from an experimental standard, with corrections for backscattering (Rc), absorption (Ac), secondary fluorescence (Fc), and continuum-generation differences (Zc). The Zc term is particularly important because the generated continuum intensity can differ substantially between a particle and its standard as a function of average atomic number, potentially varying by 20–500%. The excerpt emphasizes that the true matrix-free continuum-generation term is not simply the empirical background function fB; instead, it is calculated as Bgen = fB · S, including a stopping-power correction. For compounds, the average atomic number is computed using the Statham formulation, which outperforms simple mass-weighted alternatives and supports use of one standard per element. To address geometry artifacts in irregular particles, the conventional flat-surface X-ray path is modified with fitted geometric parameters z0 and m: ℓ(z) = (z + z·m + z0)csc Ψ. Positive parameter values represent increased absorption and negative values reduced absorption relative to a flat sample. This provides an approximate correction for surface tilt and positional offset along the detector path.

Their implementation models continuum generation, absorption, electron backscattering, and detector response, while adding geometry-dependent absorption-path corrections and low-energy attenuation corrections. contexts.context: The excerpt provides background directly relevant to correcting geometry artifacts in quantitative SEM/EDS analysis of particles and rough surfaces, although it does not describe the specific Statham–Small peak-to-background ratio method. Conventional standards-based k-value analysis assumes that both specimens and standards are flat, polished bulk targets positioned at carefully defined angles relative to the incident beam and x-ray spectrometer. Rough, irregular specimens and particles can violate these assumptions, particularly when their dimensions are comparable to electron interaction volumes and x-ray generation or propagation ranges. Such geometry differences can alter x-ray generation, absorption, and escape, producing errors in measured intensities and therefore in calculated concentrations. The authors note that spectra can still be collected from irregular specimens and analyzed using k-value or standardless procedures, but the reliability of the resulting, often normalized, concentrations must be evaluated. Their study specifically examines specimen shapes that depart from the ideal bulk geometry. The methodology uses measured standards, MLLS peak fitting, k-values, and the XPP matrix correction procedure, with high-count spectra acquired at 20 keV. This supports the general conclusion that geometry correction or a geometry-insensitive analytical approach is necessary for quantitative particle and rough-surface EDS, but the excerpt contains no equations, implementation details, or validation results for the peak-to-background ratio approach.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the peak-to-background (P/B) ratio as a method for reducing geometry-related artifacts in quantitative SEM-EDS analysis of particles. Loose powders with irregular particle sizes and morphologies produce mass and absorption effects that distort characteristic X-ray peak intensities, making conventional bulk-specimen quantification unreliable. The P/B approach addresses these effects by using the fact that characteristic peak and continuum X-rays are generated locally and are affected similarly by particle morphology. Normalizing characteristic peak intensity to the local continuum background can therefore compensate for geometry-induced variations. Earlier studies reportedly achieved relative errors of approximately 10–20% for some micron-scale particle compositions, although their applicability was limited by narrow chemistry coverage and reliance on sample-specific standards or standardless normalization. The cited excerpt does not provide specific bibliographic or procedural details about Statham and Small, nor does it explicitly describe their particular correction formulation for rough surfaces. It does, however, establish the general principle underlying geometry-artifact correction: use a locally measured background signal to normalize the elemental peak response. The article presents a newer particle-based implementation intended to improve scalability and accuracy, including analysis of light elements and use of one experimental standard per element.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a framework for interpreting microstructural heterogeneity in rapidly solidified Al-Si powder. Particle size strongly affects cooling: smaller particles have a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio, cool more rapidly, and generally reach greater undercooling. Greater undercooling increases the solidification driving force and interface velocity, so particle size can influence dendrite or cellular scale and the development of eutectic segregation. Atomization gas is also important; helium promotes faster cooling than nitrogen because of its greater heat capacity, thermal conductivity, and heat-transfer coefficient. The thermal history of an atomized droplet commonly includes an initial adiabatic stage, during which recalescence reheats the particle and the interface velocity decreases, followed by slower, approximately isothermal growth controlled by external heat loss. This change in growth conditions can produce different morphologies or segregation spacings at different positions within one particle, contributing to microstructural heterogeneity. Under sufficiently extreme undercooling, a particle can enter the hypercooled regime, where recalescence does not restore the temperature to the melting point and segregation may be absent. The excerpt does not give specific quantitative relationships for alpha-Al dendrite fraction, eutectic Si spacing, supersaturated solid solution, or cell size versus particle size, but it establishes cooling rate, undercooling, gas choice, and changing interface velocity as the controlling factors.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to microstructural heterogeneity in rapidly solidified Al-Si powder primarily through its discussion of competing nucleation pathways, growth morphologies, particle size, and cooling rate. Two dominant structures were identified: dendritic or cellular α-Al surrounded by coupled eutectic, and fully coupled eutectic growth. Aluminum nucleation produces aluminum cells or dendrites, whereas silicon nucleation can lead to small primary Si crystals that are rapidly overtaken by aluminum and do not represent a stable primary-Si growth regime. Nucleation is heterogeneous and depends on oxide-layer or internal catalytic sites, so individual particles can solidify differently even under nominally similar conditions. Across particle populations, Si nucleation becomes more likely with increasing Si content and particle size, because larger droplets are more likely to contain nucleation-promoting particles or “motes.” Cooling rate also affects heterogeneity: helium-atomized Al-15Si powder was less likely to nucleate Si than similarly sized nitrogen-atomized powder. The passage further notes that undercooling estimates derived from eutectic spacing support the conclusion that primary-Si growth is generally inaccessible in the studied powders. Although the excerpt does not provide quantitative eutectic-Si spacing laws, supersaturated solid-solution data, or a cell-size-versus-particle-size relationship, it links microstructural variation to undercooling, nucleation stochasticity, particle size, and cooling conditions.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes a framework for analyzing microstructural heterogeneity in rapidly solidified atomized Al-Si droplets. It emphasizes that a single fine droplet can contain more than one microstructure because the thermal and solute conditions at the advancing solid–liquid interface change during solidification. Depending on the evolving conditions, eutectic, dendritic, and microcellular structures may form; transitions can occur when growth conditions cross a coupled-zone boundary. Spatial measurements of eutectic spacing are particularly useful because eutectic spacing is controlled primarily by solute diffusion and capillarity and is related to the local interface velocity. Consequently, variation in spacing through a droplet can be used to infer time-dependent interface velocity and interface undercooling, thereby assessing recalescence. The study used high-pressure nitrogen gas atomization of Al-Si alloy at eutectic composition (12.6 wt% Si), with droplets separated into 12 size classes from 2 to 150 µm. Optical microscopy, SEM, and—for the finest droplets—TEM were used. The excerpt does not provide specific results for hypoeutectic alpha-Al dendrite morphology, supersaturated solid solution, quantitative cell-size-versus-particle-size relations, or cooling-rate values, but it indicates that changing thermal history, droplet size, and recalescence govern the observed microstructural scale and phase selection.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides direct evidence of microstructural heterogeneity in rapidly solidified hypoeutectic Al-Si powder and relates the observed structures to particle size. In Al-18Si powder, particles below 10 µm displayed a two-phase structure interpreted as microcellular aluminum, whereas larger particles commonly contained primary, hexagonal silicon crystals. Silicon-nucleated particles occurred across diameters above 10 µm and represented the largest overall particle fraction, but silicon dendrites were absent at every size range. Alpha-aluminum cells or dendrites generally nucleated heterogeneously on primary silicon surfaces from silicon-depleted liquid, then grew until replaced or overtaken by coupled eutectic growth. The extent of aluminum dendrite growth varied substantially, and some particles showed no intermediate dendritic growth, with eutectic growth beginning directly beside the silicon crystals. Between 10 and 37 µm, some aluminum dendrites nucleated independently of silicon, producing additional heterogeneity; their morphology was distinguishable because silicon-assisted dendrites had greater directional growth, likely due to epitaxial nucleation on faceted silicon surfaces. This excerpt does not provide quantitative eutectic silicon spacing, supersaturated solid-solution measurements, cell-size-versus-particle-size scaling, or explicit cooling-rate values, although the size-dependent transition from microcellular aluminum to primary-silicon-containing structures is relevant to those topics.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to rapidly solidified Al-Si microstructural heterogeneity, although it concerns laser surface remelting rather than hypoeutectic Al-Si powder. It reports a heterogeneous structure in which equiaxed primary alpha-Al dendrites are embedded in an ultrafine Al-Si eutectic and remain separated from one another by the eutectic. The primary Al dendrites formed within the melt pool have a reported width of 920 ± 200 nm. Rapid solidification strongly refines the eutectic Si morphology: Si changes from interconnected or flake-like structures to an interconnected network of fibers, with fiber widths of approximately 45–65 nm and a typical refined fiber width near 45 ± 10 nm. The Si inter-fiber spacing increases with scanning speed, while the fiber width is comparatively insensitive to scanning speed; at 120 mm/s, the larger spacing is attributed to fewer available nucleation sites. The ultrafine eutectic has a Si-fiber-width-to-spacing relationship near 1:1, compared with about 1:3 for the as-cast eutectic, and its measured composition is Al-21 ± 0.4 Si, slightly above the average LSR composition. The excerpt does not provide particle size, cell-size-versus-particle-size comparisons, or direct evidence for a supersaturated alpha-Al solid solution.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that rapidly solidified Al-Si powder particles can be microstructurally heterogeneous because latent-heat release produces recalescence and non-steady growth conditions during solidification. Across an individual droplet, the microstructural scale can vary substantially and the morphology may transition between eutectic, dendritic, and cellular forms. The controlling processing variables identified are particle (droplet) size, chamber cooling conditions, and heterogeneous nucleation sites. For a droplet nucleating at its surface, interface velocity, the magnitude of the thermal gradient, and cooling rate are largest near the nucleation site and decrease as solidification consumes the liquid. Thus, particle size is linked to the evolving thermal history and to the resulting length scales, although the excerpt does not provide a quantitative cell-size-versus-particle-size relationship. The paper’s stated approach is to measure spatial variations in microstructural scales and compare them with growth models to determine interface velocity and undercooling. contexts.context: The excerpt directly supports discussion of microstructural heterogeneity in rapidly solidified hypoeutectic-like Al-Si material. Laser surface remelting produces a heterogeneous structure consisting of equiaxed primary Al dendrites surrounded or separated by ultrafine Al-Si eutectic. The primary dendrites are not interconnected and have an average width of 920 ± 200 nm, while the eutectic is substantially finer than in conventional hypoeutectic material and has a measured volume fraction of 45 ± 5% in the cited heterogeneous structure. Rapid cooling near the scanning surface shifts the effective eutectic composition toward higher Si content and refines the eutectic morphology. High cooling rates also promote solute trapping, producing randomly distributed, faceted Si nano-precipitates within primary Al dendrites; these precipitates are generally smaller than 100 nm and occur more consistently near the scanning surface. Their absence farther from the surface indicates a strong cooling-rate dependence. The excerpt does not provide explicit numerical eutectic Si spacing, alpha-Al supersaturation values, cellular solidification dimensions, or a direct comparison between cell size and powder-particle size. It describes dendrite dimensions rather than powder-derived cell size, so those specific powder metrics cannot be inferred reliably from this passage.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides relevant evidence on how rapid solidification and spatially varying cooling rates influence Al-Si microstructural heterogeneity, although the study concerns laser-surface-remelted hypereutectic Al-Si rather than hypoeutectic powder. Increasing laser scan speed reduces energy input and melt-pool dimensions while increasing cooling rate. Within one melt pool, cooling rate varies with depth because laser power density decreases exponentially downward: the bottom experiences lower cooling rates, while the region near the scanning surface experiences higher cooling rates. The microstructure changes correspondingly from fully eutectic ultrafine Al-Si in the pool center to heterogeneous Al-Si near the upper region. In the rapidly solidified heterogeneous regions, primary alpha-Al dendrites contain Si nanoprecipitates. The excerpt contrasts this with coarse as-cast eutectic Si flakes, whose average width is 1.3 ± 0.4 μm and interflake spacing is 4.4 ± 1.8 μm; laser remelting produces Si fibers with much finer dimensions. Importantly, the highest cooling rate does not necessarily produce the finest eutectic Si: the finest Si fibers occur in the fully eutectic middle region rather than near the surface. The passage does not provide powder-specific cell size versus particle size data or direct evidence for supersaturated alpha-Al solid solution.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes microstructural heterogeneity in rapidly solidified hypoeutectic Al–Si particles, specifically Al–3 wt% Si and Al–6 wt% Si. Particles in the 0.1–1.0 μm range commonly exhibited three successive microstructural regions. Initially, rapid growth produced a supersaturated α-Al solid solution with a planar interface, followed by precipitation of very fine Si clusters. During recalescence, reduced solute-trapping capability created a segregate-free zone and increased Si supersaturation ahead of the interface. As solidification progressed, the planar interface became unstable and transformed into a cellular structure, providing qualitative evidence for cell formation and microstructural heterogeneity. Smaller particles were more likely to remain segregation-free because they experienced greater undercooling and higher solid/liquid interface velocities; conversely, large faceted Si crystals were more frequently observed in larger, higher-Si particles. The excerpt does not provide a direct quantitative cell-size-versus-particle-size relationship or explicit cooling-rate data for these powders. It does state that eutectic, microcellular, and dendrite-arm spacings can be used as indirect measures of interface temperature and velocity. Jackson–Hunt and TMK models relate eutectic spacing to growth velocity and undercooling, with the TMK extension being more appropriate when rapid solidification raises the Peclet number above unity.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides comparative particle-size and composition-related observations for water-atomized (WA) and gas-atomized (GA) alloy 625 powders, but it does not directly discuss particle-size/composition correlation, segregation during storage in containers, or powder sampling procedures such as splitting or riffling. WA powder generally has a broader and larger particle-size distribution than GA powder. Optical analysis measured WA particles from 3.8 to 84.6 µm with an average of 41.9 µm, whereas GA particles ranged from 3.9 to 61.9 µm with an average of 29.7 µm. Laser diffraction produced similar average sizes—34.5 µm for WA and 33.0 µm for GA—but again showed a wider WA distribution. Three-dimensional optical analysis reported D50 values of 15.54 µm for WA and 24.84 µm for GA, while circularity was substantially lower for WA (0.755) than GA (0.957), indicating less spherical particles. The authors attribute differences in thermal behavior partly to chemical composition, median particle size, and oxygen/carbon contents. TGA behavior suggests more carbide/Laves-related dissolution in WA, while GA had little or no detectable Laves, γ′′, or NbC precipitation and was described as higher-purity powder with composition closer to nominal. These findings may support investigating whether size fractions differ chemically, but the excerpt does not present fraction-specific chemical analyses.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides relevant guidance for investigating particle-size composition and obtaining representative samples of atomized alloy powder, but it does not directly discuss correlations between chemical composition and particle diameter or segregation within containers. For powder sampling, it states that a rotary sample divider produces substantially lower standard deviation than chute splitting (0.146% versus 1.01%), indicating that rotary division is preferred for reducing sampling variability. It also explains that the minimum gross-sample mass depends on powder density, allowable sampling error, the mass fraction of the coarsest size class, and the characteristic particle diameter; ISO 3081 recommends a minimum incremental mass of 0.3 kg for material with a maximum particle size of 10–0 mm. Particle-size distribution can be determined by classification or sieve analysis. Sieve analysis is described as the predominant method for metal powders larger than 5 μm: a stacked series of sieves is arranged from largest opening to smallest, the powder is shaken, and the retained material on each sieve is weighed to calculate size fractions. These procedures could support separate chemical analysis of size-separated fractions, but the excerpt does not specify how alloying elements vary with particle size or how container segregation should be measured.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to sampling atomized alloy powders and evaluating possible relationships between particle-size composition and measured chemical or technological properties. It states that powder behavior and properties can depend on granulometric composition, particle shape and morphology, specific surface, and moisture. Representative sampling is essential because unreliable samples can produce misleading chemical-composition and physical-property data. Segregation may occur in packaged or transported powders, particularly near the surface of truck or wagon loads because of vibration; increments should therefore be taken at least 300 mm below the surface. For stored powders, containers should be selected systematically or preferably by randomization, and multiple increments are combined into a gross or composite sample before testing. Sample reduction methods include conical pouring and quartering, chute splitting, and rotary sample division (riffling/dividing). The reported reliability comparison favors mechanical division: quartering and scoop sampling had standard deviations of 6.81% and 5.14%, chute splitting 1.01%, and rotary division only 0.146%. The excerpt does not directly establish a chemical-composition-versus-particle-diameter correlation, but it emphasizes that particle-size distributions and segregation must be controlled to obtain valid composition measurements.

It explains that particle-size fractions are commonly made wider as particle size increases because surface-area differences become less significant for coarse particles. When constructing a weight-based particle-size histogram using unequal fraction ranges, the percentage in each fraction should be divided by that fraction’s size interval; this produces a clearer representation of the powder’s disperse composition. The text also emphasizes that powder properties depend strongly on surface area, which may be important when considering whether chemical composition or behavior varies with particle diameter. For chemical composition, the excerpt lists bulk methods such as atomic absorption, ICP-OES, X-ray fluorescence, XRPD, and inert-gas fusion; microanalysis methods include SEM with EDS and electron microprobe analysis. SEM/EDS can provide qualitative analysis of individual particles, while microprobe analysis provides quantitative microchemical information. X-ray diffraction can quantify phases, generally with sensitivity around 3–5 vol%, and transmission electron microscopy can examine specific phases and their particle size, shape, and crystallographic orientation. These techniques could support investigation of composition differences among particle-size fractions, although no direct particle-diameter/composition correlation is reported here.
